title: Must-Practice Designs
description: End-to-end production system design blueprints following the 7-step framework: 1. Requirement Gathering, 2. Scale Assumption, 3. QPS/Memory/5-Year Storage Estimation, 4. API Design & Entities + ER Diagram, 5. High-Level Box Diagram, 6. Deep Dive Flows 1 & 2, and 7. Further Improvements.

subtopics.title: URL Shortener
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a Bitly/TinyURL-scale shortening and redirection service with Base62 encoding, distributed ID generation, and sub-10ms global redirects.
keyTakeaways: A 7-character Base62 string ([0-9a-zA-Z]) yields 62^7 = 3.52 trillion unique codes—enough for 100+ years at 1,000 writes/sec without collisions.
Pre-generating counter ranges via ZooKeeper/etcd or using 64-bit Snowflake IDs encoded in Base62 completely eliminates write-path database contention and hash-collision retries.
Use HTTP 301 (Permanent) when minimizing origin server load via browser caching is top priority, or HTTP 302 (Temporary) when real-time click analytics and dynamic link target updates are required.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A URL Shortener converts long, unwieldy URLs (such as marketing links with UTM parameters) into compact aliases (e.g., `https://sho.rt/2bX9kLm`) and redirects users to the original destination with near-zero latency.
bullets: Functional Requirement 1 — URL Shortening: Given a valid `longUrl`, generate a unique 7-character Base62 `shortCode`. Support optional user-defined `customAlias` (up to 16 chars) and configurable `expiresAt` TTL.
Functional Requirement 2 — Redirection: Given `GET /{shortCode}`, redirect the client via HTTP 301 or 302 to the original `longUrl`, or return HTTP 404/410 if not found or expired.
Functional Requirement 3 — Link Management & Basic Analytics: Allow authenticated users to deactivate links and asynchronously record click counts, referrers, and geo-regions.
Non-Functional Requirement 1 — Ultra-Low Read Latency: Redirection (`GET /{shortCode}`) p99 latency must be < 10ms inside the data center (< 50ms globally via CDN edge).

Non-Functional Requirement 2 — High Availability (AP over CP on Reads): 99.99% uptime for redirection (< 52 minutes downtime/year). Eventual consistency (~100ms replication lag) is acceptable for newly created links, except custom aliases which require strong uniqueness.
Out of Scope: Full user registration/OAuth provider implementation, real-time ad-bidding on interstitial pages, and deep HTML scraping of destination pages.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: Before estimating hardware, we establish realistic production traffic parameters modeled after a tier-1 URL shortening platform.
bullets: Monthly Active Users (MAU): 500 Million users clicking shortened links globally; 50 Million Daily Active Users (DAU) generating or clicking links.
Write Volume (New URLs Created): 100 Million new shortened URLs created per day.
Read:Write Ratio: 100:1 (Read-heavy workload — 10 Billion redirects per day across web, SMS, and social platforms).
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 3x average traffic during major global events or marketing campaigns.

Average Object Size: `shortCode` (7 bytes) + `longUrl` (500 bytes average, up to 2,048 bytes max) + `userId` (8 bytes) + `createdAt` / `expiresAt` / metadata (64 bytes) ≈ 600 bytes raw (~1 KB with DB index and row overhead).
Data Retention Policy: 5 years default retention for links unless explicitly extended by enterprise accounts.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Using powers-of-ten back-of-the-envelope math (1 day ≈ 86,400 seconds ≈ 10^5 seconds), we size our compute, memory, storage, and network tiers.
bullets: Write QPS: 100M writes / 86,400 sec ≈ 1,160 Writes/sec average; Peak Write QPS (3x) ≈ 3,500 Writes/sec.
Read QPS: 10B reads / 86,400 sec ≈ 115,740 Reads/sec average; Peak Read QPS (3x) ≈ 350,000 Reads/sec.

5-Year Storage: 100M URLs/day × 365 days × 5 years = 182.5 Billion URLs. At 1 KB per record (including indexes), raw storage = 182.5 TB. With 3x replication factor across Availability Zones = ~550 TB.

Redis Cache Memory (80/20 Pareto Rule): Caching 20% of daily active URLs absorbs 80%+ of read traffic. 20% of 100M daily active distinct URLs = 20M hot entries × 1 KB (including Redis dict/ziplist pointers) ≈ 20 GB minimum; to cache 20% of an entire month's active links (600M links × 1 KB) = ~600 GB RAM across a 16-node Redis Cluster.
Network Bandwidth: Ingress (writes) = 3,500 peak QPS × 1 KB = 3.5 MB/s (28 Mbps). Egress (reads) = 350,000 peak QPS × 1 KB HTTP response headers = 350 MB/s (2.8 Gbps).

                  URL SHORTENER CAPACITY ESTIMATION SHEET
================================================================================
1. TRAFFIC & QPS (1 Day = 86,400 seconds ≈ 100,000 seconds)
   - Daily Writes (New URLs)    : 100,000,000 (100M / day)
   - Average Write QPS          : 100M / 86,400      = ~1,160 QPS
   - Peak Write QPS (3x)        : 1,160 * 3          = ~3,500 QPS
   - Daily Reads (Redirects)    : 10,000,000,000 (10B / day, 100:1 ratio)
   - Average Read QPS           : 10B / 86,400       = ~115,740 QPS
   - Peak Read QPS (3x)         : 115,740 * 3        = ~350,000 QPS

2. SHORT CODE KEYSPACE MATH (Base62 = [0-9, a-z, A-Z])
   - 6 characters : 62^6 = 56.8 Billion unique keys
   - 7 characters : 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 (3.52 Trillion unique keys)
   - Required for 5 years       : 100M/day * 365 * 5 = 182.5 Billion URLs
   -> Decision: 7-char Base62 provides ~19x headroom over 5-year requirement.

3. 5-YEAR PERSISTENT STORAGE
   - Record Size                : ~600B payload + ~400B index/metadata = 1 KB
   - Total Records (5 Years)    : 1.825 * 10^11 records (182.5B)
   - Raw Storage                : 182.5B * 1 KB      = 182.5 TB
   - Replicated Storage (RF=3)  : 182.5 TB * 3       = 547.5 TB (~550 TB)

4. REDIS CACHE MEMORY (RAM)
   - Daily Hot Set (20% of 100M): 20M keys * 1 KB    = 20 GB RAM
   - 30-Day Hot Working Set     : 600M keys * 1 KB   = 600 GB RAM
   - Cluster Topology           : 10 Primary + 10 Replica nodes (64 GB RAM each)

5. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Ingress (Write)       : 3,500 QPS * 1 KB   = 3.5 MB/sec  (28 Mbps)
   - Peak Egress (Read)         : 350,000 QPS * 1 KB = 350 MB/sec  (2.8 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: We separate the Write Path (URL creation) and Read Path (Redirection) into independently scalable microservices so a sudden 10x spike in viral link clicks never starves URL creation.
bullets: Edge CDN & API Gateway: Terminates TLS, blocks malicious IPs, enforces per-IP rate limits, and caches 301 redirects directly at Cloudflare/CloudFront PoPs.
Write Service & Ticket Server (ZooKeeper/etcd or Snowflake): Allocates collision-free 64-bit numeric IDs and converts them to Base62 without querying the database first.

Read (Redirect) Service with 2-Tier Cache: Uses an in-process L1 Caffeine cache (10,000 hottest celebrity links with 5s TTL) plus a distributed L2 Redis Cluster (600 GB RAM) to serve 99% of reads without touching disk.
Async Analytics Pipeline: The Redirect Service pushes click events non-blockingly to Kafka, which Flink aggregates into ClickHouse for real-time dashboards.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let's trace the two most critical engineering flows in detail: Flow 1 (Collision-Free Short URL Creation via Distributed Range/Base62 Encoding) and Flow 2 (High-Throughput Cache-Aside Redirection with Cache Stampede & Penetration Protection).
bullets: Flow 1 (Write Path — Base62 + Range Allocator): Rather than hashing the URL with MD5/SHA256 (which suffers from birthday-paradox collisions when truncated to 7 chars and requires expensive DB uniqueness checks), each Write Service node leases a block of 100,000 sequential 64-bit integers from etcd/ZooKeeper in memory. Incrementing an `AtomicLong` takes 2 nanoseconds and guarantees 0% collision.

Preventing Predictable Sequential URLs: To prevent competitors from scraping sequential URLs (`abc1234`, `abc1235`), we apply a fast bijective XOR/Feistel permutation or multiplicative inverse (`(id * PRIME) & MASK`) on the 64-bit integer before Base62 encoding.

Flow 2 (Read Path — Multi-Level Caching & Bloom Filter): A redirect request checks L1 (Caffeine) -> L2 (Redis) -> L3 (Cassandra). To prevent malicious bots from querying millions of random non-existent codes (Cache Penetration), a Redis Bloom Filter rejects unknown codes before hitting Cassandra.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To harden the system from a textbook architecture into a globally resilient production service, we address security, hot keys, and multi-region failover.
bullets: Malicious Link & Phishing Prevention: Integrate Google Safe Browsing API and PhishTank checks synchronously (using local bloom filter snapshots updated every 15 minutes) and asynchronously on the write path to auto-disable phishing or malware links.

Celebrity Hot-Key Mitigation: If a link tweeted by a celebrity receives 200,000 QPS, a single Redis shard could saturate its network NIC. The L1 in-memory Caffeine cache (5-second TTL) in each Redirect Service pod absorbs 99.9% of single-key spikes before they hit Redis.

Multi-Region Active-Active Reads & Writes: Deploy Write and Redirect services across `us-east-1`, `eu-west-1`, and `ap-southeast-1`. Assign disjoint ID ranges per region (or region bits in Snowflake) and replicate mappings globally via DynamoDB Global Tables or multi-DC Cassandra (`NetworkTopologyStrategy`).

Graceful Expiration & Tombstone Compaction: Rather than running expensive batch `DELETE` jobs that create tombstones in LSM-tree databases, leverage native Cassandra/DynamoDB item-level TTLs so expired links are purged automatically during routine SSTable compaction.

tradeOffs.option: Base62 Encoding of Sequential/Snowflake ID
tradeOffs.pros: Zero collision probability; no database read needed before write; predictable fixed 7-char length.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires a distributed range coordinator (etcd/ZooKeeper) or clock synchronization (Snowflake); sequential IDs must be scrambled to prevent enumeration.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput production URL shorteners (Bitly, TinyURL) where write latency and zero collisions are paramount.

tradeOffs.option: Truncated Cryptographic Hash (First 7 chars of MD5/SHA-256)
tradeOffs.pros: Stateless generation; identical long URLs can naturally deduplicate to the same short code.
tradeOffs.cons: High birthday-paradox collision rate as DB fills up; requires check-then-set DB round-trips or appending random salts on collision.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Small-scale internal link deduplicators where identical URLs must map to the exact same alias.

tradeOffs.option: HTTP 301 (Permanent) vs. HTTP 302 (Temporary) Redirect
tradeOffs.pros: 301 offloads repeat clicks to browser & CDN caches (lowest latency & server cost); 302 forces every click through the Redirect Service.
tradeOffs.cons: 301 blinds server-side click analytics for repeat visitors and prevents updating the destination URL once cached by browsers.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Use 301 for static, unmonetized links; use 302 (default for Bitly) when click analytics or dynamic link retargeting are required.

subtopics.interviewTip: Never propose `SELECT MAX(id) + 1` or plain UUIDv4 truncation without discussing collisions. Immediately walk the interviewer through Base62 math (`62^7 = 3.52 trillion`), explain how a ZooKeeper/etcd range allocator leases blocks of 100,000 IDs to each app server in memory, and proactively contrast HTTP 301 vs. 302 for analytics vs. caching.

subtopics.title: Rate Limiter
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a distributed, sub-millisecond API rate limiting middleware using Redis Lua scripts, Token Bucket, and Sliding Window algorithms.
keyTakeaways: Token Bucket is the industry standard for API gateways because it allows controlled traffic bursts up to bucket capacity while enforcing a steady-state refill rate using only two values per key (`tokens` and `lastRefillTimestamp`).
Check-then-set race conditions in distributed Redis rate limiters MUST be eliminated by executing the token refill and decrement logic inside a single atomic Redis Lua script (`EVALSHA`).

A production rate limiter must fail-open (or fall back to local in-memory Token Buckets) if the Redis cluster experiences a network partition, preventing a rate-limiter outage from taking down the entire platform.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A Distributed Rate Limiter sits at the edge (API Gateway) or service mesh sidecar to protect backend microservices from cascading failures, noisy-neighbor tenants, brute-force credential stuffing, and runaway billing costs.
bullets: Functional Requirement 1 — Multi-Dimensional Throttling: Throttle requests based on flexible keys: authenticated `userId`, `apiKey`, client `ipAddress`, or route-specific keys (e.g., `POST /api/v1/login` limited to 5 req/min per IP).

Functional Requirement 2 — Dynamic Rule Management: Support hierarchical, hot-reloadable rate-limit rules per customer tier (e.g., Free: 100 req/min, Pro: 5,000 req/min, Enterprise: 50,000 req/min with custom burst capacity).

Functional Requirement 3 — Standard HTTP Headers & Status: Reject excess traffic with `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests` and populate `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` (`Retry-After`) headers on every response.
Non-Functional Requirement 1 — Sub-Millisecond Latency Overhead: The rate-limiting check stands in the critical path of every API call and must complete in < 1ms p95 and < 2ms p99.

Non-Functional Requirement 2 — High Availability & Fault Tolerance: If the distributed state store (Redis) becomes unreachable, the rate limiter must gracefully degrade (fail-open or switch to local per-pod memory limits) rather than dropping 100% of user traffic.
Out of Scope: Layer-3/Layer-4 volumetric SYN flood mitigation (handled upstream by Cloudflare/AWS Shield) and billing invoice generation.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: Since the rate limiter inspects every incoming API request across the entire organization, its QPS equals the aggregate ingress traffic of the platform.
bullets: Daily Active Users (DAU) & Devices: 100 Million active users/devices and 500,000 B2B API keys.
Average Requests per User per Day: 100 API calls/user/day → 10 Billion total API checks per day.
Read:Write Ratio: 1:1 Atomic Read-Modify-Write — every incoming API check reads current token state, calculates elapsed refill, and decrements the token count in one atomic operation.
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 5x average traffic during flash sales, market opens, or DDoS/bot scraping waves.

State Footprint per Active Bucket: Key (`rl:{user_id}:{route_id}` ≈ 32 bytes) + `tokens` (8-byte float/int) + `last_refill_ms` (8-byte int64) + Redis hash-table metadata (56 bytes) ≈ 104 bytes (~128 bytes per active bucket).

Rule Retention & Bucket TTL: Rate-limit rules are stored permanently in PostgreSQL (< 10,000 rules). Ephemeral Redis token buckets automatically expire via TTL after the window duration (e.g., 1 hour max idle).

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: We calculate the Redis cluster throughput, memory footprint for millions of concurrent rate-limit buckets, and 5-year audit/analytics storage.
bullets: Average Check QPS: 10B requests / 86,400 sec ≈ 115,740 checks/sec.
Peak Check QPS (5x): 115,740 × 5 ≈ 580,000 checks/sec (~600K QPS across the Redis Cluster).

Redis Memory Footprint: Suppose 20% of the 100M DAU are active within any rolling 1-hour TTL window across an average of 3 distinct rate-limited endpoints = 20M users × 3 buckets = 60 Million active buckets. At 128 bytes/bucket = 60M × 128B ≈ 7.68 GB RAM. Even if all 100M DAU have 5 active buckets simultaneously, 500M × 128B = 64 GB RAM!

Redis Shard Sizing for 600K Peak QPS: A single Redis instance comfortably handles ~80,000–100,000 Lua `EVALSHA` ops/sec. To serve 600,000 QPS with < 50% CPU utilization headroom, we deploy 12 Redis Primary shards (+ 12 Replicas).

5-Year Storage (Rule Store + Throttle Audit Logs): Rules DB in Postgres is tiny (< 50 MB). However, if we log 1% sampled throttled (`HTTP 429`) security events for abuse forensics (assume 2% of 10B daily requests are throttled = 200M/day; 1% sample = 2M events/day × 250 bytes × 365 × 5 years) ≈ 912.5 GB (~2.7 TB with 3x replication).
Network Bandwidth: 600,000 peak QPS × 150 bytes (Redis RESP protocol command + response) = 90 MB/s (720 Mbps) internal east-west traffic between API Gateways and Redis.

   - Worst-Case Peak RAM        : 100M DAU * 5 buckets * 128B = ~64 GB RAM

   - 5-Year Replicated (RF=3)   : 912.5 GB * 3            = ~2.74 TB

4. INTERNAL NETWORK BANDWIDTH (Gateway <-> Redis Cluster)
   - Request + Response Payload : ~150 Bytes (EVALSHA + 4 args + array reply)
   - Peak Bandwidth             : 600,000 QPS * 150 Bytes = 90 MB/sec (720 Mbps)

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: To achieve < 1ms latency, the Rate Limiter runs as an embedded library/filter inside the API Gateway (or Envoy sidecar) rather than a separate network hop, talking directly to the Redis Cluster via persistent connection pools.
bullets: In-Memory Rule Cache: Gateways never query PostgreSQL on the request path. A background daemon subscribes to Redis Pub/Sub (or polls every 30s) to keep the active `RateLimitRule` tree in local JVM memory.
Sharded Redis Cluster: Uses consistent hashing (CRC16 mod 16384 slots) over the subject key (`rl:{ruleId}:{subjectId}`) so all checks for a specific user route to the exact same Redis primary shard.

Local Resilience Fallback (Circuit Breaker): Resilience4j monitors Redis call latency. If Redis times out (> 5ms) or fails, the filter trips its circuit breaker and switches to a local in-memory ConcurrentHashMap Token Bucket divided by the number of gateway pods.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: We examine two core implementation flows: Flow 1 (Atomic Distributed Token Bucket in Redis Lua vs. Sliding Window Counter) and Flow 2 (Gateway Filter Execution with Circuit-Breaker Failover and HTTP Header Injection).
bullets: Why Naive Redis `GET` then `SET` Fails: If two concurrent requests from `user_123` arrive at two different Gateway pods at `t = 100ms` when `tokens = 1`, both pods `GET` `tokens = 1`, both allow the request, and both write `tokens = 0`. A Redis Lua script executes single-threaded inside the Redis shard, guaranteeing strict serializability with 1 network round-trip.

Algorithm Comparison: Fixed Window suffers from the 2x boundary burst problem (100 requests at `00:59` + 100 requests at `01:01` = 200 requests in 2 seconds). Sliding Window Log (Redis `ZSET`) is exact but consumes O(N) memory per request. Token Bucket and Sliding Window Counter use O(1) memory (2 numbers per key).

Flow 2 (Resilient Gateway Enforcement): Evaluates the Redis Lua script via pre-loaded SHA1 digest (`EVALSHA`), attaches `X-RateLimit-*` headers, and falls back to an in-memory Caffeine bucket if Redis throws a timeout exception.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: At ultra-high scale (millions of QPS), even a single Redis round-trip per request can become a bottleneck for hot global keys.
bullets: Local Token Batching (Quota Leasing) for Hot Keys: For global or high-tier enterprise API keys making 50,000 req/sec, each API Gateway pod leases batches of 500 tokens at a time from Redis and decrements them locally in JVM memory, cutting Redis network calls by 99.8%.

Clock Skew Elimination via `redis.call('TIME')`: In the Lua script, instead of passing `now_ms` from the Gateway JVM (where NTP drift between 50 gateway pods can cause negative `elapsed_sec`), call Redis's internal `redis.call('TIME')` so all time math uses the single shard's monotonic clock.

Shadow Mode (Dry-Run) Rollouts: When introducing a new rate-limit rule in production, deploy it with `mode = SHADOW` first so the gateway logs would-be `429` events to ClickHouse/Prometheus without actually blocking live customer traffic.

Multi-Layer Defense (L4 + L7 + Concurrency Limiters): Combine token-bucket rate limiting with adaptive concurrency limiting (Netflix Gradient2 / Little's Law `maxInFlight`) to protect downstream services when their latency spikes.

tradeOffs.option: Token Bucket (2 fields per key in Redis Hash)
tradeOffs.pros: O(1) memory (128 bytes/key); naturally accommodates legitimate traffic bursts up to bucket capacity; easy to weight expensive endpoints with higher token cost.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires atomic read-modify-write via Lua script (`EVALSHA`).
tradeOffs.bestFor: General-purpose API gateways (Stripe, AWS API Gateway, Kong) where burst tolerance and low memory footprint are critical.

tradeOffs.option: Sliding Window Log (Redis Sorted Set `ZSET`)
tradeOffs.pros: 100% mathematically exact across any rolling window boundary; never allows 2x boundary spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: O(N) memory footprint—storing 10,000 timestamps for an enterprise user consumes ~640 KB per user; `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` becomes expensive.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Strict low-volume security endpoints (e.g., max 5 failed login or OTP attempts per 15 minutes).

tradeOffs.option: Sliding Window Counter (Weighted Hybrid of 2 Fixed Windows)
tradeOffs.pros: O(1) memory (only 2 integers: previous window count and current window count); approximates sliding window with 99.997% accuracy.
tradeOffs.cons: Slightly less intuitive for burst modeling compared to explicit bucket capacity + refill rate.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Cloudflare-scale edge rate limiting where simple atomic counters (`INCR`) and minimal memory are desired.

subtopics.interviewTip: Interviewers will almost always ask: 'What happens if two Gateway servers check Redis at the exact same millisecond?' Draw the race condition and immediately write or explain the atomic Redis Lua script (`EVALSHA`). Then score bonus Staff+ points by mentioning `redis.call('TIME')` to solve NTP clock skew across gateway nodes and fail-open circuit breaking when Redis is down.

subtopics.title: Distributed Cache
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a multi-terabyte, sub-millisecond in-memory caching cluster with Consistent Hashing, Segmented LRU/W-TinyLFU eviction, and singleflight stampede protection.
keyTakeaways: Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes (vnodes) limits key remapping to ~1/N of the dataset when a cache node joins or crashes, preventing catastrophic database cache-miss avalanches.

Inside a single cache node, combining a ConcurrentHashMap with a Segmented Doubly-Linked List (or W-TinyLFU admission filter) enables O(1) lookups and evictions without global lock contention across CPU cores.

Production caches must defend against the Three Cache Killers: Cache Stampede (solved via Singleflight request coalescing + early probabilistic recomputation), Cache Penetration (negative caching / Bloom filters), and Hot Keys (L1 client-side near-cache).

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: We are designing a high-throughput, low-latency Distributed In-Memory Cache (similar to Redis Cluster or Memcached with Mcrouter) that sits in front of slower disk-based databases to serve millions of operations per second.
bullets: Functional Requirement 1 — Core Key-Value Operations: Support `get(key)`, `set(key, value, ttlMs)`, `delete(key)`, and atomic `compareAndSet(key, expectedVersion, newValue)` with binary byte-array values up to 1 MB.

Functional Requirement 2 — Automatic Eviction & Expiration: Enforce both lazy expiration (on read) and active background TTL sweeps, plus bounded-memory eviction via Segmented LRU or W-TinyLFU when shard memory reaches capacity.

Functional Requirement 3 — Dynamic Cluster Partitioning & Failover: Partition keys across shards via Consistent Hashing (or 16,384 hash slots) and automatically promote a replica shard within seconds if a primary node crashes.
Non-Functional Requirement 1 — Sub-Millisecond Latency: `GET` and `SET` p99 latency must be < 1ms within the same Availability Zone.
Non-Functional Requirement 2 — High Availability & Linear Scalability: Scale horizontally to 10+ Million QPS and 10+ TB of aggregate RAM with minimal key movement (`~1/N` keys) during node scaling.
Out of Scope: Complex multi-key ACID transactions across shards, secondary SQL-like indexing, and long-term durable archival.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the distributed cache for a tier-1 e-commerce or social platform caching user sessions, product catalogs, and social graph edges.
bullets: Daily Active Users (DAU): 200 Million DAU generating heavy read traffic across microservices.
Aggregate Cache Traffic: 150 Billion cache operations per day across all internal microservices.
Read:Write Ratio: 10:1 (`GET` vs `SET`/`DELETE`) — ~136 Billion reads/day and ~14 Billion writes/day.
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 3x average traffic during prime evening hours.
Average Cached Entry Size: Key (64 bytes) + Value (compressed JSON/Protobuf payload averaging 2 KB) + Hash node/LRU pointers & TTL metadata (64 bytes) ≈ 2.13 KB per entry.
Working Set Size: 3 Billion unique active keys held in memory simultaneously across the cluster (with TTLs ranging from 5 minutes to 24 hours).

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Let's compute the cluster-wide QPS, total RAM required across shards, replication overhead, and network NIC saturation limits.
bullets: Read QPS: 136B reads / 86,400 sec ≈ 1,574,000 Reads/sec average; Peak Read QPS (3x) ≈ 4.72 Million Reads/sec.
Write QPS: 14B writes / 86,400 sec ≈ 162,000 Writes/sec average; Peak Write QPS (3x) ≈ 486,000 Writes/sec (~5.2M total Peak QPS).

Total Cluster Memory (RAM): 3 Billion keys × 2.13 KB ≈ 6.39 TB of raw cached data. Accounting for 20% memory fragmentation and eviction headroom (`maxmemory` at 80%), primary RAM = 8 TB. With 1 read replica per primary shard for HA (RF=2), total cluster RAM = 16 TB.

Shard Count Calculation: Using `r6g.2xlarge` instances with 64 GB RAM (50 GB usable per node), 8 TB / 50 GB = 160 Primary Shards + 160 Replica Shards = 320 cache nodes. Each primary shard handles 5.2M / 160 = ~32,500 Peak QPS (well below the ~100K QPS single-core saturation limit).

5-Year Persistent Storage (AOF / RDB Snapshots for Warm Restart): Although a cache is ephemeral, storing periodic RDB snapshots on S3/EBS for fast cold-boot recovery requires 8 TB × 3 daily snapshots retained = 24 TB.
Network Bandwidth: Peak Egress = 4.72M Read QPS × 2 KB = 9.44 GB/sec (75.5 Gbps across 160 shards = ~472 Mbps per node, easily handled by 10 Gbps NICs).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: A Distributed Cache system consists of three cooperative planes: the Smart Client Router (Consistent Hash Ring + L1 Cache + Singleflight), the Data Plane (Segmented In-Memory Storage Shards), and the Control Plane (Cluster Membership & Auto-Failover).
bullets: Consistent Hash Ring Router: Hashes keys using MurmurHash3 (32-bit or 64-bit) onto a circular ring `[0, 2^32 - 1]`. Each physical shard owns 150 Virtual Nodes on the ring to guarantee uniform standard deviation (< 5% load variance across shards).

Segmented In-Memory Engine: Instead of a single global `synchronized` LRU lock that serializes all threads on a 16-core machine, each shard partitions its keyspace into 16 independent `CacheSegment` instances (by `hash(key) & 15`), each with its own lock and doubly-linked LRU list.

Primary-Replica Replication & Control Plane: Writes go to the Primary shard and replicate asynchronously to its Replica shard. etcd/ZooKeeper (or Redis Cluster Gossip) monitors heartbeats and triggers replica promotion on failure.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let's dive into the exact Java implementation of Flow 1 (Consistent Hashing Router + Singleflight Cache Stampede Prevention on the Client) and Flow 2 (Thread-Safe Segmented LRU + TTL Eviction Engine on the Server).
bullets: Flow 1 (Consistent Hashing + Singleflight Coalescing): When a popular cache key expires under 10,000 concurrent requests/sec, naive Cache-Aside triggers 10,000 simultaneous SQL queries (Cache Stampede / Thundering Herd). Using `ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<byte[]>>` (`inFlightLoads`), the first thread queries the DB while the other 9,999 threads await the exact same `CompletableFuture`.

Flow 2 (O(1) Segmented LRU + Active/Lazy Expiration): On `get(key)`, if the entry is expired (`now >= expireAtMs`), it is unlinked and removed lazily. If valid, it is moved to the `head` of its segment's doubly-linked list in O(1) time. On `put(key, val)`, if `currentBytes > maxSegmentBytes`, entries are evicted from `tail.prev` (Least Recently Used) until space is freed.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To operate a multi-terabyte cache cluster without cascading outages, we add defenses against cache scan pollution, inconsistent writes, and cold-cache restarts.
bullets: W-TinyLFU Eviction (Scan Resistance): Pure LRU suffers from cache pollution when a batch job scans millions of one-off keys, flushing genuinely hot items. Upgrading the eviction policy to W-TinyLFU (Window-TinyLFU with a Count-Min Sketch frequency filter, as used in Caffeine) rejects one-hit wonders from evicting high-frequency keys.

Cache-Aside + Delete-on-Write vs. CDC Invalidation: When the database updates, having the application execute `DB.update()` followed by `Cache.delete(key)` can still suffer from a rare race if a slow concurrent reader repopulates stale data. Coupling Debezium (Kafka CDC on the database WAL/binlog) to issue idempotent cache invalidations guarantees eventual convergence within milliseconds.

Hot-Key Client-Side Near-Caching (Redis v6 Client-Side Tracking): For extreme hot keys (e.g., homepage config read 500,000 times/sec), cache the value in the application JVM's local L1 cache and use Redis RESP3 Client-Side Caching invalidation messages (`CLIENT TRACKING`) to evict L1 entries when mutated.

Slab Allocation / Off-Heap Memory (`ByteBuffer.allocateDirect`): In Java/JVM-based cache servers, storing 64 GB of byte arrays on the JVM heap causes multi-second GC stop-the-world pauses. Allocate cache payloads off-heap using Netty `PooledByteBufAllocator` or slab arenas (like Memcached) to eliminate GC pressure.

tradeOffs.option: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading + Delete on DB Write)
tradeOffs.pros: Resilient to cache failures; only requested data is cached; application has full control over serialization and TTLs.
tradeOffs.cons: First request for any key suffers a cache-miss penalty (3 hops); vulnerable to thundering herd on hot-key expiration unless paired with Singleflight.
tradeOffs.bestFor: 90% of general read-heavy microservice workloads (user profiles, product catalogs, feed metadata).

tradeOffs.option: Read-Through / Write-Through Cache
tradeOffs.pros: Cache is always warm after writes; simplifies application code by abstracting the database behind the cache API.
tradeOffs.cons: Every write pays the latency of updating both cache and DB synchronously; pollutes cache with write-once data that may never be read.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Workloads where newly written records are guaranteed to be read immediately and repeatedly.

tradeOffs.option: Write-Behind (Write-Back) Caching
tradeOffs.pros: Fastest possible write latency (writes hit RAM only) and enables batching/coalescing rapid counter updates before flushing to DB.
tradeOffs.cons: Risk of data loss if both primary and replica cache shards crash before the async queue flushes to disk.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-velocity counters, view/like tallies, and gaming state where transient loss of a few seconds is acceptable or backed by Redis AOF.

subtopics.title: Notification System
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a multi-channel (APNs, FCM, Email, SMS) notification engine with priority queues, deduplication, user preference filtering, and exponential backoff.
keyTakeaways: Strictly isolate High-Priority transactional notifications (2FA OTPs, payment alerts) from Low-Priority marketing blasts using dedicated Kafka topics and independent worker pools so a 50M-user promo campaign never delays an OTP.

External third-party providers (APNs, FCM, Twilio, SendGrid) have unpredictable latencies and rate limits; workers must decouple ingestion from delivery using per-channel Kafka queues, circuit breakers, and tiered retry topics with exponential backoff.

Guarantee at-least-once delivery with near-zero duplicate user experience by enforcing an `idempotencyKey` at ingestion and checking a Redis deduplication ledger immediately before dispatching to the external provider.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A centralized Notification System provides a unified API for internal services to send multi-channel notifications (iOS Push, Android Push, Web Push, SMS, and Email) while respecting user preferences, quiet hours, and provider rate limits.
bullets: Functional Requirement 1 — Multi-Channel & Priority Routing: Support Push (APNs, FCM), SMS (Twilio/AWS SNS), and Email (AWS SES/SendGrid) across 3 priority tiers: `CRITICAL` (OTPs, fraud alerts), `HIGH` (chat messages, order updates), and `BULK` (marketing digests).

Functional Requirement 2 — User Preferences, Quiet Hours & Device Management: Check per-user, per-channel opt-in/opt-out settings and local timezone quiet hours (e.g., suppress non-critical push between 10 PM and 8 AM local time) before sending.

Functional Requirement 3 — Templating, Deduplication & Delivery Tracking: Render localized templates (`en_US`, `es_ES`), deduplicate retried client requests via `idempotencyKey`, and record delivery lifecycle states (`PENDING`, `SENT`, `DELIVERED`, `FAILED`, `CLICKED`).

Non-Functional Requirement 1 — Priority Latency SLAs: `CRITICAL` (P0) notifications must be dispatched to the external provider within < 500ms p99; `BULK` (P2) notifications can be delivered within minutes.

Non-Functional Requirement 2 — Reliability (At-Least-Once Delivery, Zero Lost OTPs): 99.99% ingestion availability; resilient retries with exponential backoff when third-party providers (Twilio/FCM) experience brownouts.
Out of Scope: Building a custom SMTP mail transfer agent from scratch or cellular telecom tower routing.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We model a global consumer platform (like Uber, DoorDash, or Amazon) sending transactional and promotional notifications across ratusan of millions of users.
bullets: Daily Active Users (DAU): 100 Million DAU (with an average of 2 registered mobile devices per user = 200M device tokens).
Daily Notification Volume by Channel: 1 Billion Mobile Push notifications/day + 200 Million Emails/day + 50 Million SMS messages/day = 1.25 Billion total notifications/day.
Read:Write Ratio: Write-heavy pipeline (1.25B notification dispatches/day + ~2.5B status/webhook updates/day; ~1.25B preference/device-token cache reads/day).
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 5x average traffic during breaking news, flash sales, or top-of-the-hour scheduled digest crons.
Average Payload Size: Push/SMS request payload + metadata ≈ 1 KB; Email rendered HTML payload ≈ 25 KB; Delivery log record in Cassandra/ClickHouse ≈ 500 bytes.
Data Retention Policy: Notification delivery logs and audit history retained for 90 days in hot storage and 5 years in compressed analytical/cold storage.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Let's calculate the dispatch QPS per channel, Redis memory for preferences and deduplication keys, and 5-year storage for notification history.
bullets: Push QPS: 1B / 86,400 sec ≈ 11,574 Push/sec average; Peak Push QPS (5x) ≈ 58,000 Push/sec.
Email QPS: 200M / 86,400 sec ≈ 2,315 Emails/sec average; Peak Email QPS (5x) ≈ 11,600 Emails/sec.
SMS QPS: 50M / 86,400 sec ≈ 579 SMS/sec average; Peak SMS QPS (5x) ≈ 2,900 SMS/sec (Total Peak Dispatch ≈ 72,500 notifications/sec).

Redis Memory (User Preferences + Device Tokens + 24h Idempotency Keys): 100M DAU × 500 bytes (device tokens + channel bitmask + timezone) = 50 GB RAM. Plus 1.25B daily idempotency keys (`idem:{uuid}` -> 1-byte status, 64 bytes overhead) with 24-hour TTL = 80 GB RAM. Total Redis Cluster RAM = ~130 GB (with replicas = 260 GB).

5-Year Storage (Notification Delivery Logs): 1.25B notifications/day × 500 bytes per log entry = 625 GB/day. Over 5 years (1,825 days) = 1.14 PB raw. With 3x replication in Cassandra (for 90-day hot window = 168 TB) and Zstd-compressed Parquet on S3 (4:1 compression ratio for 5-year archive) = ~168 TB hot DB + ~285 TB S3 cold archive.
Network Bandwidth: Peak Egress = (58,000 Push × 1 KB) + (2,900 SMS × 1 KB) + (11,600 Email × 25 KB) = 58 MB/s + 2.9 MB/s + 290 MB/s ≈ 351 MB/s (2.8 Gbps).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture separates Ingestion & Routing from Channel Delivery using priority-isolated Kafka topics (`notif.p0.*`, `notif.p1.*`, `notif.p2.*`) and tiered retry queues.
bullets: Priority Queue Isolation: P0 (`CRITICAL`), P1 (`HIGH`), and P2 (`BULK`) notifications flow through completely separate Kafka topics and consumer groups. Even if Marketing enqueues 50 Million P2 emails at 9:00 AM, P0 OTP workers have zero lag.

Channel-Specific Worker Pools: APNs workers maintain persistent HTTP/2 mTLS connection pools to Apple; FCM workers batch up to 500 tokens per HTTP/2 call; SMS workers manage multi-vendor routing (Twilio primary, AWS SNS fallback).
Webhook & Feedback Loop Processor: Receives delivery receipts and `Unregistered` token errors from APNs/FCM/Twilio, updating Cassandra status and deactivating stale device tokens.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: We trace Flow 1 (Idempotent Ingestion, User Preference & Quiet-Hours Filtering, and Priority Topic Fan-Out) and Flow 2 (Resilient Worker Dispatch with Multi-Vendor Failover, Exponential Backoff Retry Topics, and Stale Token Cleanup).
bullets: Flow 1 (Ingestion & Preference Evaluation): Uses Redis `SET key val NX EX 86400` on `request.idempotencyKey()` to reject duplicate API retries at the door. Resolves the user's local hour from their IANA timezone (`ZoneId.of(pref.timezone())`) and suppresses `HIGH`/`BULK` notifications during quiet hours while always allowing `CRITICAL` OTPs through.

Flow 2 (Worker Dispatch, Multi-Vendor Failover & Tiered Retries): Before calling the external provider, the worker checks a channel-specific deduplication key (`sent:{idempotencyKey}:{channel}`). If Twilio returns `503` or times out, P0 SMS immediately fails over to secondary vendor AWS SNS; P1/P2 notifications publish to `notif.retry.1m` with exponential backoff and jitter.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To prevent notification fatigue, provider blacklisting, and runaway SMS costs, production notification platforms add intelligent safeguards.
bullets: Per-User Frequency Capping (Anti-Spam): Maintain a sliding window counter in Redis (`freq:{userId}:{channel}`) that caps non-critical notifications to at most 3 push notifications per hour and 5 per day, coalescing excess updates into a single summary digest.

Outbox Pattern for Transactional Guarantees: Calling services (like `OrderService`) can write notification events into a local transactional `outbox` table in the same ACID transaction as the order update, streamed to Kafka via Debezium CDC so no notification is ever lost on network blip.

Dynamic Provider Health & Cost Routing: Continuously track per-country SMS delivery success rates and latency across Twilio, Sinch, Infobip, and AWS SNS. Automatically shift traffic away from degraded carriers using an adaptive weighted bandit router.

Token Hygiene & Bounce Feedback Loops: Process AWS SES bounce/complaint SNS webhooks and APNs `410 Unregistered` responses in real time to immediately scrub invalid emails/device tokens—protecting sender IP reputation from ISP blacklisting.

tradeOffs.option: Strict Priority Topic Isolation (`notif.p0.*` vs `notif.p2.*`)
tradeOffs.pros: Complete bulkheads—a 100M-user marketing blast in P2 can never delay a P0 2FA OTP; worker autoscaling can be tuned independently per priority.
tradeOffs.cons: 3x more Kafka topics and consumer groups to provision and monitor.
tradeOffs.bestFor: All production notification systems mixing real-time transactional alerts (OTPs, payments) with scheduled marketing campaigns.

tradeOffs.option: Tiered Kafka Retry Topics (`retry.1m`, `retry.5m`, `retry.30m`) vs. In-Thread Sleep
tradeOffs.pros: Never blocks active consumer threads waiting on a failing message; preserves high throughput for healthy recipients while delaying only failed dispatches.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires forwarding messages across multiple topics before reaching the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput event-driven delivery pipelines interacting with flaky external HTTP APIs.

tradeOffs.option: Render Templates at Ingestion vs. Render in Channel Workers
tradeOffs.pros: Rendering in Channel Workers keeps Kafka message payloads tiny (~300 bytes of template variables instead of 25 KB HTML emails) and avoids wasted CPU if a message is later deduplicated or dropped.
tradeOffs.cons: If a template is modified while messages sit in a backlog queue, queued messages render the newer template version unless template versions are pinned.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-volume email and multi-locale push pipelines where Kafka broker disk and network I/O must stay lean.

subtopics.interviewTip: In a Notification System interview, immediately draw the boundary between P0 (Transactional OTPs) and P2 (Marketing Bulk) queues. Walk through how a marketing blast would starve OTPs in a single FIFO queue, explain how `idempotencyKey` + Redis `SETNX` prevents duplicate SMS charges, and mention handling APNs `410 Unregistered` feedback to clean up dead device tokens.

subtopics.title: Chat System
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a WhatsApp/Discord-scale real-time messaging platform with stateful WebSockets, hybrid group fan-out, monotonic message ordering, and offline inbox sync.
keyTakeaways: Maintain persistent, stateful bidirectional WebSocket connections on Netty Chat Gateways, backed by a Redis Session Registry mapping `userId -> gatewayNodeId` for instant cross-node message routing.

Use per-conversation monotonic sequence numbers (or time-ordered Snowflake IDs) as the Cassandra clustering key `(channel_id, message_id)` so clients can deterministically order messages and sync missed offline history via `WHERE message_id > lastSeenMsgId`.

Use Hybrid Fan-Out for group chats: Push-on-Write (fan-out to each member's active WebSocket/inbox) for small groups (<= 500 members like WhatsApp), and Pull/PubSub-on-Read for massive 100K-member Discord channels.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: We are designing a real-time 1-on-1 and Group Chat System (combining the core capabilities of WhatsApp and Slack/Discord) supporting instant delivery, multi-device synchronization, offline inbox catch-up, and online presence indicators.
bullets: Functional Requirement 1 — 1-on-1 & Group Messaging: Support real-time text and media-metadata messaging for 1-on-1 chats and group channels (up to 500 members for standard groups; up to 50,000 members for community channels).

Functional Requirement 2 — Delivery Lifecycle & Multi-Device Sync: Track `SENT`, `DELIVERED`, and `READ` receipts (`lastReadMessageId` watermark) and synchronize message history seamlessly across up to 5 linked devices per user (Phone, Web, Desktop).

Functional Requirement 3 — Online Presence & Offline Push Fallback: Broadcast online/last-seen status to active conversation partners and automatically deliver APNs/FCM push notifications when a recipient has no active WebSocket connection.
Non-Functional Requirement 1 — Real-Time Delivery Latency: End-to-end message delivery latency between two online users must be < 100ms p99 globally.

Non-Functional Requirement 2 — Strict Per-Channel Ordering & Durability: Zero message loss once acknowledged (`SENT`). Messages within the same `channelId` must appear in a consistent, deterministic order across all participants.
Out of Scope: Peer-to-peer WebRTC video/voice calling media relays (TURN/STUN servers) and client-side Signal Protocol cryptographic key-exchange math.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size our architecture for a massive global messaging platform with 100 Million Daily Active Users.
bullets: Daily Active Users (DAU): 100 Million DAU; Peak Concurrent Connected Users (CCU): 50 Million active WebSocket connections open simultaneously.
Daily Message Volume: Each DAU sends 40 messages/day = 4 Billion messages created per day.

Fan-Out Delivery Multiplier: Including 1-on-1 chats (1 recipient) and group chats (average 4 recipients per message across the platform), each written message fans out to 4 recipients on average = 16 Billion message deliveries per day.
Read:Write Ratio: 4:1 on the real-time delivery path (16B deliveries vs 4B writes), plus 4B presence heartbeats/day.
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 3x average traffic during major holidays, sports finals, or regional peak hours.

Average Message Size: `messageId` (8B) + `channelId` (8B) + `senderId` (8B) + `content` (200 bytes average text) + metadata/attachments JSON (150 bytes) ≈ 400 bytes raw (~500 bytes including Cassandra row/index overhead). Media files (images/videos) are uploaded directly to S3 via pre-signed URLs.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: We compute the write QPS, fan-out delivery QPS, stateful WebSocket gateway fleet size, Redis session memory, and 5-year Cassandra message storage.
bullets: Write QPS (Messages Sent): 4B messages / 86,400 sec ≈ 46,300 Writes/sec average; Peak Write QPS (3x) ≈ 140,000 Writes/sec.
Delivery QPS (WebSocket Fan-Out): 16B deliveries / 86,400 sec ≈ 185,200 Deliveries/sec average; Peak Delivery QPS (3x) ≈ 555,000 Deliveries/sec.

Stateful WebSocket Gateway Sizing: Using Java Netty (epoll/NIO non-blocking sockets), each TCP connection consumes ~15 KB of kernel + JVM buffer memory. One gateway server handles 100,000 concurrent WebSockets (~1.5 GB socket memory on a 16 GB RAM node). For 50 Million peak concurrent connections: 50,000,000 / 100,000 = 500 Netty Chat Gateway pods.

Redis Session & Presence Memory: 50M concurrent users × 2 active devices = 100M active session mappings (`sess:{userId}` -> Hash of `deviceId -> gatewayNodeId` + `lastHeartbeatMs`, ~200 bytes per user) = 20 GB RAM. Adding active group membership caches (50M active groups × 500 bytes) = 25 GB RAM. Total Redis Cluster RAM = ~50 GB Primary (100 GB with replicas).

5-Year Persistent Message Storage (Cassandra): 4B messages/day × 500 bytes = 2 TB/day. Over 5 years (1,825 days) = 3.65 PB raw storage. With 3x replication factor across Availability Zones = ~10.95 PB (~11 PB).

Network Bandwidth: Peak Ingress = 140,000 Write QPS × 500 bytes = 70 MB/sec (560 Mbps). Peak Egress = 555,000 Delivery QPS × 500 bytes = 277.5 MB/sec (2.22 Gbps) + Presence Heartbeats (50M users / 30s interval = 1.67M pings/sec × 64 bytes = 107 MB/s).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The key architectural insight of a Chat System is separating the Stateful Connection Layer (Netty WebSocket Gateways holding open TCP sockets) from the Stateless Business Logic Layer (Chat Routing Service, Group Manager, Presence Service).
bullets: Netty WebSocket Connection Gateways: Lightweight, connection-focused servers that terminate TLS/WebSocket connections, maintain an in-memory map of `localSockets: Map<DeviceKey, Channel>`, and forward incoming frames via gRPC to the Chat Routing Service.
Redis Session & Presence Cluster: Maps every online user's connected devices (`sess:{userId}` -> `{deviceId: gatewayId}`) with a 60-second TTL refreshed by 30-second client heartbeats.
Apache Cassandra / ScyllaDB Cluster: LSM-tree columnar store optimized for high-velocity sequential writes and range scans (`message_id > X`) without B-tree random I/O amplification.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: We trace Flow 1 (End-to-End Real-Time Message Send, Persistence, Multi-Device Routing & Offline Push Fallback) and Flow 2 (Offline Reconnection Inbox Sync & Hybrid Large-Group Fan-Out).
bullets: Flow 1 (Send & Multi-Device Fan-Out): User A sends a message over WebSocket to `gw-12`. `gw-12` forwards it to `ChatRoutingService`, which assigns a 64-bit Snowflake `messageId`, persists it to Cassandra, returns `SERVER_ACK` to User A, and looks up all devices for both User A (to sync User A's iPad/Web client!) and User B in Redis. Online devices receive the frame immediately via gRPC to their respective Gateway nodes; offline mobile devices receive an APNs/FCM push.

Flow 2 (Reconnection Catch-Up & Hybrid Group Fan-Out): When a user comes out of an airplane or subway tunnel and reconnects, their client sends `lastSeenMessageId` per active channel and executes a fast Cassandra range scan (`WHERE channel_id = ? AND bucket_yyyymm = ? AND message_id > ?`). For mega-groups (> 500 members, e.g., 50K Discord channel), instead of copying the message to 50,000 user inboxes on write, the message is written once to `channel_messages` and broadcast to the Gateway nodes via a Redis Pub/Sub topic `channel:{channelId}`.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To scale a real-time chat system to billions of messages without presence storms or reconnection avalanches, we implement production optimizations.
bullets: Presence Fan-Out Throttling (Solving the Presence Storm): Broadcasting every user's online/offline heartbeat to all 500 of their contacts generates O(N^2) traffic. Instead, use explicit viewport subscriptions: a client only subscribes to real-time presence updates for the 10–15 users currently visible on their screen or inside an open chat window.

End-to-End Encryption (Signal Double Ratchet Protocol): For private 1-on-1 and small group chats, store Pre-Keys (`IdentityKey`, `SignedPreKey`, `OneTimePreKeys`) on a Key Directory Service so clients encrypt payloads locally before sending over WebSocket; Cassandra stores only opaque ciphertext.

Thundering Herd Reconnection Jitter: If a regional load balancer blips and drops 1 Million WebSocket connections simultaneously, all 1M mobile clients reconnecting at the exact same millisecond will crush TLS handshakes and Redis session writes. Enforce client-side randomized exponential backoff with full jitter (`sleep = random(0, min(30s, 2^attempt))`).

Media Offloading via Pre-Signed S3 + CDN: Never pipe multi-megabyte photos or voice notes through the stateful WebSocket gateways. Clients request a pre-signed S3 upload URL via HTTPS, upload the encrypted binary directly to S3, and send only the lightweight `mediaUrl` + thumbnail hash inside the WebSocket frame.

tradeOffs.option: WebSockets (Bidirectional Persistent TCP) vs. HTTP Long Polling / SSE
tradeOffs.pros: True full-duplex low-latency communication with minimal framing overhead (~2 bytes per frame header) for both client-to-server sends and server-to-client pushes.
tradeOffs.cons: Stateful connections require L7 connection-aware load balancing, sticky session registries in Redis, and careful connection draining during deployments.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time bidirectional chat apps (WhatsApp, Discord, Slack) with high-frequency message sends, typing indicators, and read receipts.

tradeOffs.option: Snowflake 64-bit IDs vs. Per-Channel Monotonic Auto-Increment Counter
tradeOffs.pros: Snowflake IDs are generated statelessly without cross-node coordination and are naturally K-sorted by time across all channels.
tradeOffs.cons: Snowflake IDs do not provide contiguous gap-free integers (`1, 2, 3`), so detecting a missing message requires watermark comparison rather than checking `seq == prevSeq + 1`.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Globally distributed chat systems where write scalability across millions of concurrent channels outweighs strict gapless integer numbering.

tradeOffs.option: Push-on-Write (Small Groups <= 500) vs. Pull/PubSub (Mega-Groups > 500)
tradeOffs.pros: Push-on-Write gives instant per-device delivery and offline push notifications for personal groups; Gateway Pub/Sub avoids looking up 100,000 user sessions in Redis on every message in a massive community channel.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires maintaining two routing code paths based on channel `member_count`.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Platforms supporting both private group chats and massive public channels (Discord, Telegram, Slack Enterprise).

subtopics.interviewTip: Always clarify maximum group size early! Explaining why you use direct per-member session lookup in Redis for WhatsApp-sized groups (<= 500 members) vs. Gateway-level Pub/Sub for 50,000-member Discord channels—and how Cassandra's composite key `((channel_id, bucket_yyyymm), message_id DESC)` prevents unbounded wide partitions—immediately signals Staff-level depth.

subtopics.title: News Feed
subtopics.subtitle: Hybrid Fanout-on-Write / Fanout-on-Read Timeline Engine, Celebrity Hot-Key Mitigation & ML Ranking Pipeline
keyTakeaways: Use a Hybrid Fanout strategy: push (fanout-on-write) post IDs into Redis ZSET timelines for regular users (< 50,000 followers), and pull (fanout-on-read) dynamically at query time for high-follower 'celebrity' accounts.
Store only lightweight references (`(postId, authorId, createdAt)` = 24 bytes) in the user's timeline cache, hydrating full post & user metadata in bulk via a pipelined L1/L2 cache layer.
Use cursor-based pagination (`max_timestamp` / Snowflake ID) instead of `OFFSET/LIMIT` so scrolling remains deterministic and duplicate-free even as new posts arrive at the top of the feed.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A News Feed system (like X/Twitter, Instagram, or LinkedIn) aggregates posts from followed users, topics, and communities into a personalized, low-latency stream. The central engineering tension is handling extreme fanout asymmetry when accounts with tens of millions of followers publish content.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Users can publish posts containing text, media URLs, and hashtags; (2) Users can follow/unfollow other users; (3) Users can fetch their home timeline ordered chronologically or by relevance score with cursor pagination; (4) Real-time engagement counters (likes, replies, reposts) appear on timeline cards.

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Availability: 99.99% AP system (eventual consistency of 1–5 seconds for new posts appearing in followers' feeds is acceptable); (2) Latency: P99 < 200ms for timeline generation and hydration, P99 < 150ms for publishing a post; (3) Celebrity Fanout SLA: A post from a user with 50M followers must be visible to active readers within 2 seconds without exhausting cluster write IOPS.
Out of Scope: Direct messaging, ad auction bidding mechanics, raw video transcoding pipelines (handled by an external Media Service), and full-text search indexing.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: News feeds are heavily read-skewed in terms of user requests, yet write-amplified internally due to follower fanout.
bullets: Traffic & User Base: 1 Billion MAU, 300 Million DAU.
Write Traffic: Each DAU publishes an average of 2 posts/day -> 600 Million new posts/day.
Read Traffic: Each DAU opens or refreshes their home feed 20 times/day (fetching 20 posts per page) -> 6 Billion timeline read requests/day.
Read-to-Write Ratio: 10:1 at the API edge (6B reads vs 600M writes), though each write triggers an average fanout to 200 followers.
Peak Multiplier: 3x average traffic during breaking global events (World Cup, elections).
Average Payload Sizes: Post metadata + text = 1 KB; Timeline cache entry (`post_id` + `author_id` + `timestamp_score`) = 24 bytes; Media stored externally on Object Storage/CDN.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: We separate edge API QPS from internal fanout write QPS, and size the Redis cluster to retain the latest 800 post references for every active user.
bullets: Write QPS (Edge): 600M posts / 86,400 sec ≈ 6,944 writes/sec average; Peak Write QPS (3x) ≈ 21,000 posts/sec.

Internal Fanout Write QPS: With 200 average followers per user, naive fanout = 6,944 × 200 ≈ 1.39M Redis ZADD ops/sec average (4.17M ops/sec peak). Hybrid fanout cuts celebrity writes, keeping internal fanout under 1.5M ops/sec at peak.
Read QPS: 6B timeline requests / 86,400 sec ≈ 69,444 reads/sec average; Peak Read QPS (3x) ≈ 210,000 reads/sec.

Redis Timeline Cache Memory: Keep top 800 post entries per user for 300M DAU + 200M warm users (500M users total). Each entry = 24 bytes + ~16 bytes Redis ZSET skiplist overhead = 40 bytes. Per user = 800 × 40 B = 32 KB. Total Timeline RAM = 500M × 32 KB = 16 TB (32 TB with 1 replica per shard).
Post Metadata Cache Memory: Cache hot posts from the last 3 days (3 × 600M = 1.8B posts × 20% hot ratio = 360M posts) × 1 KB = 360 GB RAM.
5-Year Persistent Storage: 600M posts/day × 1 KB = 600 GB/day -> 219 TB/year -> 1.095 PB over 5 years. With 3x Cassandra/ScyllaDB replication + 30% B-Tree/LSM index overhead ≈ 4.27 PB.
Bandwidth: Ingress = 21,000 peak writes/sec × 1 KB = 21 MB/sec (168 Mbps); Egress = 210,000 peak reads/sec × (20 posts × 1 KB) = 4.2 GB/sec (33.6 Gbps).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture decouples the synchronous write path from asynchronous follower fanout using Kafka, while the read path combines precomputed user inbox timelines with on-the-fly celebrity outbox merges.
bullets: API Gateway & Auth Layer: Terminates TLS, validates JWT tokens, enforces per-user rate limits, and routes traffic to Post Service or Feed Service.

Post Service & Cassandra/ScyllaDB Cluster: Generates Snowflake IDs, writes posts to the durable wide-column store (`posts_by_id` and `posts_by_author`), updates the author's Redis outbox (`outbox:{authorId}`), and publishes a `PostCreatedEvent` to Kafka.

Social Graph Service: Stores `followers` and `following` lists in sharded ScyllaDB tables cached in Redis, tagging celebrity edges so the Feed Service can quickly identify which celebrities a reader follows.

Fanout Worker Pool: Consumes `PostCreatedEvent` from Kafka. If the author has `< 50,000` followers, workers fetch follower IDs in pages and issue pipelined Redis `ZADD inbox:{followerId}` + `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` (capping at 800 entries).

Feed Service & Hydration Cache: On read, fetches the user's `inbox:{userId}` ZSET, queries the `outbox:{celebId}` ZSETs for followed celebrities, merges and sorts candidate post IDs, optionally runs a lightweight ML ranker, and bulk-hydrates post/user objects via `MGET` against the Post & User Cache.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Below we trace the two core operational flows: (Flow 1) Hybrid Fanout-on-Write when a post is published, and (Flow 2) Hybrid Timeline Read, K-Way Merge, and Pipelined Cache Hydration.
bullets: Flow 1 — Hybrid Write & Fanout Path: When an author posts, the Post Service persists the post and writes its reference to `outbox:{authorId}`. When the Kafka Fanout Worker processes the event, it inspects `author.isCelebrity()`. If `true`, it skips follower fanout entirely (saving millions of Redis writes). If `false`, it streams follower IDs from the Social Graph Service (filtering out inactive users who haven't logged in for >30 days) and executes pipelined Lua scripts to insert into `inbox:{followerId}` and trim entries beyond index 800.

Flow 2 — Hybrid Read, Merge & Hydration Path: When `userId` requests their feed with `cursor` (last seen Snowflake `postId`), the Feed Service concurrently (a) reads `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE inbox:{userId} (cursor -inf LIMIT 0 40` and (b) fetches the list of celebrities `userId` follows (`celeb_following:{userId}`) and pipelines `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE outbox:{celebId} (cursor -inf LIMIT 0 10` for each. It merges the two streams using a bounded PriorityQueue (Min-Heap of size `limit`), and finally hydrates the winning 20 `postId`s via a single batched Redis `MGET` with ScyllaDB fallback.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: Taking a News Feed from a working prototype to a planetary-scale social network requires defending against viral hot keys, optimizing cache memory, and integrating ML ranking without violating the 200ms P99 budget.
bullets: Viral Post Hot-Key Mitigation (L1 Local Caffeine Cache): When a celebrity posts a viral update, millions of readers simultaneously request hydration for the exact same `postId`. A single Redis shard holding that `post:{postId}` key can saturate its 100K ops/sec single-core limit. Each Feed Service instance maintains a 2-second TTL in-memory L1 `Caffeine` cache for top viral posts and celebrity `outbox:{celebId}` slices, absorbing 99% of hot-key reads inside JVM memory.

Cold User Eviction & Lazy Timeline Reconstruction: Pushing fanout writes to 700M inactive users wastes ~22 TB of Redis RAM. Only fan out to users active within the last 14–30 days. If a dormant user logs back in (cache miss on `inbox:{userId}`), trigger a fallback Fanout-on-Read query across their followed accounts to warm their inbox lazily.

Two-Stage ML Ranking Pipeline: For 'For You' algorithmic feeds, split ranking into Stage 1 (Retrieval/Candidate Generation collecting ~1,000 candidates from Graph Inbox, Topic Embeddings, and Trending pools in <30ms) and Stage 2 (Heavy Neural Ranker scoring those 1,000 candidates on GPU/ONNX inference servers in <60ms) before hydrating the top 20.

Read-Your-Own-Writes Consistency: Because Kafka fanout and celebrity cache propagation take 100ms–2s, the Feed Service always merges the caller's own `outbox:{callerUserId}` into their home timeline so a newly published post appears instantaneously at the top of the author's screen.

Graceful Degradation & Circuit Breaking: If the ML Ranking Service or Engagement Counter Service times out (>80ms), the Feed Service falls back to reverse-chronological Snowflake order with cached/approximate counter values rather than failing the timeline request.

tradeOffs.option: Pure Fanout-on-Write (Push Model)
tradeOffs.pros: O(1) timeline read latency from precomputed Redis ZSET; read path is completely decoupled from the number of accounts a user follows.
tradeOffs.cons: Massive write amplification for celebrity accounts (1 post -> 50M Redis writes), causing severe fanout lag and wasted RAM for inactive followers.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Social networks with hard caps on connections (e.g., early Facebook 5,000-friend limit) or small private group feeds.

tradeOffs.option: Pure Fanout-on-Read (Pull Model)
tradeOffs.pros: Zero write amplification on post creation; publishing a post is a single O(1) database write regardless of follower count.
tradeOffs.cons: Slow and expensive read path: every timeline load must query hundreds of followed authors' outboxes and perform a massive K-way merge.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Write-heavy telemetry streams or niche forums where users follow very few entities and read infrequently.

tradeOffs.option: Hybrid Fanout (Push Regular + Pull Celebrities)
tradeOffs.pros: Combines sub-50ms timeline reads with bounded write amplification; eliminates celebrity hot-write storms.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher implementation complexity on the read path (merging precomputed inbox ZSET with dynamic celebrity outbox ZSETs and deduplicating).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large-scale asymmetric social graphs like X/Twitter, Instagram, Threads, and TikTok.

subtopics.interviewTip: Do not jump straight to 'Hybrid Fanout' as a buzzword—quantify *why* Pure Push fails first: show the interviewer that a celebrity with 50M followers publishing one post triggers 50M Redis writes, which at 1M ops/sec takes 50 seconds of queue lag. Then introduce the 50,000-follower threshold and explain how the reader merges their precomputed Inbox ZSET with followed Celebrity Outbox ZSETs at read time.

subtopics.title: File Storage
subtopics.subtitle: Dropbox / Google Drive Architecture: Content-Defined Chunking (Rabin Fingerprinting), CAS Deduplication & Delta Sync
keyTakeaways: Split files on the client into variable-size 4 MB–8 MB chunks using Content-Defined Chunking (Rabin Karp rolling hash) so inserting bytes at the start of a file only mutates a single chunk instead of shifting every subsequent chunk boundary.

Store chunks in Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) indexed by their `SHA-256` hash: before uploading raw bytes, the client calls a `precheck` API with its chunk hash list and only uploads chunks the server does not already possess.
Separate the Metadata Control Plane (sharded PostgreSQL/CockroachDB tracking file trees, versions, and chunk manifests) from the Data Plane (presigned direct uploads/downloads against S3/GCS).

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A cloud file storage and synchronization system (like Dropbox, Google Drive, or OneDrive) enables users to store files reliably in the cloud and keep folders synchronized across multiple devices in near real-time with minimal bandwidth consumption.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Upload and download files up to 50 GB with resumable transfer support; (2) Automatic differential sync (modifying 10 KB inside a 1 GB file should only upload/download the modified ~4 MB chunk); (3) File versioning and rollback to historical revisions; (4) Real-time multi-device sync notifications and deterministic conflict resolution (e.g., generating 'Conflicted Copy' on concurrent offline edits); (5) File and folder sharing with ACL permissions (`OWNER`, `EDITOR`, `VIEWER`).

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Durability: 99.999999999% (11 nines) for stored file blocks—zero data loss; (2) Consistency: Strong ACID consistency for file metadata, directory trees, and revision histories; (3) Availability: 99.99% for sync and download operations; (4) Bandwidth Efficiency: Global content-addressable deduplication and Zstandard compression.
Out of Scope: Real-time character-by-character collaborative document editing (like Google Docs OT/CRDTs, which is a separate service) and virus scanning implementation details.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the system for a large consumer and enterprise user base where metadata operations (polling, cursor checks, small delta edits) outnumber raw gigabyte transfers.
bullets: User Base: 500 Million registered users, 100 Million DAU (connected across an average of 2.5 devices per user = 250M active client connections).
File Inventory: Average user stores 200 files -> 100 Billion total files in the system.
Write/Sync Traffic: Each DAU creates or modifies 10 file revisions/day -> 1 Billion file revision writes/day.
Read/Download Traffic: 2 Billion file/chunk downloads or sync pulls/day (Read:Write ratio = 2:1).

Chunking & Payload Profile: Average file size = 2 MB (median is smaller, skewed by photos/videos). Files are split into variable-size chunks averaging 4 MB. Average modified delta per sync = 1 chunk (1.5 MB compressed). Global deduplication + compression saves ~40% of raw storage.
Peak Multiplier: 2.5x average traffic at 9:00 AM business-hour logins.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: We calculate QPS for metadata transactions, Redis memory for active device session routing and hot directory metadata, and 5-year multi-petabyte object storage.
bullets: Metadata Write QPS (File Revisions): 1B revisions / 86,400 sec ≈ 11,574 writes/sec average; Peak Write QPS (2.5x) ≈ 29,000 QPS.
Metadata Read QPS (Sync Cursor Checks & Manifest Fetches): 2B downloads + 3B cursor polls / 86,400 sec ≈ 57,870 reads/sec average; Peak Read QPS ≈ 145,000 QPS.

Redis Memory (Device Connection Registry + Metadata Cache): (a) 250M active device SSE/WebSocket sessions × 128 bytes (`device_id -> gateway_node_ip, workspace_id`) = 32 GB; (b) Hot file/folder metadata cache for 100M DAU (top 50 active file records × 500 bytes) = 2.5 TB. With replication, a 5.5 TB Redis cluster suffices.

5-Year Block Storage (S3/GCS): 1B daily edits × 1.5 MB average new delta = 1.5 PB/day raw. With 40% CAS deduplication + Zstd compression -> 900 TB/day net new blocks -> 328.5 PB/year -> 1.64 Exabytes over 5 years (stored across S3 Standard and Glacier Instant Retrieval with erasure coding).

5-Year Metadata Database Storage: 100B existing files + (1B revisions/day × 1,825 days = 1.825T revisions). Keeping 10 recent revisions hot and compacting older ones -> ~400B rows × 300 bytes = 120 TB raw -> 360 TB with 3-way Raft replication (CockroachDB/Spanner).

Bandwidth: Peak Upload Ingress = 29,000 writes/sec × 1.5 MB = 43.5 GB/sec (348 Gbps, handled directly by S3 edge endpoints via presigned URLs); Metadata API Bandwidth = 145,000 QPS × 2 KB = 290 MB/sec (2.32 Gbps).

FILE STORAGE (DROPBOX / DRIVE) CAPACITY WORKSHEET (100M DAU / 100B FILES)
================================================================================
1. METADATA & SYNC THROUGHPUT (QPS)
   - Avg File Revision Writes : 1,000,000,000 / 86,400      = 11,574 QPS
   - Peak Revision Writes     : 11,574 * 2.5                = 28,935 QPS
   - Avg Metadata/Sync Reads  : 5,000,000,000 / 86,400      = 57,870 QPS
   - Peak Metadata/Sync Reads : 57,870 * 2.5                = 144,675 QPS

2. REDIS MEMORY (SESSION REGISTRY + HOT METADATA CACHE)
   - Active Device Sessions   : 250M devices * 128 B        = 32 GB
   - Hot File Metadata Cache  : 100M DAU * 50 files * 500 B = 2.50 TB
   - Total Redis Cluster (2x) : (2.532 TB) * 2 (Replica)    = 5.06 TB RAM

3. 5-YEAR STORAGE (METADATA DB vs. CAS BLOCK OBJECT STORAGE)
   - Daily Raw Delta Ingress  : 1B edits * 1.5 MB           = 1.50 PB / day
   - Net Daily CAS (40% Dedup): 1.50 PB * 0.60              = 900 TB / day

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture enforces a strict separation between the Metadata Control Plane and the Binary Data Plane. Application servers never proxy raw file bytes.
bullets: Smart Client Agent (File Watcher + Rabin Chunker + Local SQLite): Monitors OS filesystem events (`FSEvents` on macOS, `inotify` on Linux), splits modified files using Content-Defined Chunking (Rabin rolling hash), compresses chunks with `Zstd`, computes `SHA-256` digests, and persists local sync state in SQLite.
Metadata & Sync Service: Stateless Java service managing directory trees, ACLs, CAS block deduplication lookups, and atomic revision commits against CockroachDB.
Cloud Object Storage (S3 / GCS CAS Bucket) & CDN: Stores immutable compressed blocks keyed by `/cas/{hash[0..3]}/{sha256_hash}`. Clients upload and download directly via short-lived Presigned URLs.
S3 Event Notification + Verification Worker: When a client finishes a presigned `PUT` to S3, S3 emits an `ObjectCreated` event to Kafka/SQS, marking the block `VERIFIED` in the `cas_blocks` table.

Notification Service (SSE / WebSocket Gateway): Subscribes to workspace commit events via Redis Pub/Sub and pushes lightweight invalidation pings (`{workspaceId, latestLsn}`) to connected devices so they immediately pull the delta manifest.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: We examine the two defining mechanisms of a modern cloud drive: (Flow 1) Content-Defined Chunking (Rabin Fingerprinting) + CAS Upload with Deduplication, and (Flow 2) Multi-Device Delta Sync with Optimistic Concurrency Conflict Resolution.
bullets: Flow 1 — Content-Defined Chunking & CAS Deduplication Upload: Why not split files at fixed 4 MB offsets? Because inserting 1 byte at index 0 of a 100 MB file shifts every single 4 MB boundary by 1 byte, invalidating all 25 chunk hashes! Instead, the client slides a 48-byte window across the file computing a Rabin-Karp polynomial rolling hash. Whenever `rollingHash & 0x3FFFFF == 0` (which happens on average every $2^{22} = 4\text{ MB}$, bounded between `MIN_CHUNK = 2 MB` and `MAX_CHUNK = 8 MB`), it declares a chunk boundary based *purely on local byte content*. Subsequent chunks remain 100% identical and are skipped via the server's CAS precheck.

Flow 2 — Multi-Device Delta Sync & OCC Conflict Resolution: Each workspace maintains a monotonically increasing Log Sequence Number (`latest_lsn`). When Device A commits version 5 of `report.pdf` (based on `expectedBaseVersion = 4`), the database executes an atomic compare-and-swap. If Device B was offline and later tries to commit its own edits also claiming `expectedBaseVersion = 4`, the OCC check sees `currentVersion == 5 != 4`. Instead of overwriting Device A's work or failing silently, the server branches Device B's revision into a new sibling file node `report (Device B's conflicted copy 2026-09-30).pdf` so zero user work is ever lost.
