sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: Operating an exabyte-scale cloud storage engine requires strict security around content-addressable deduplication, storage tiering, and LAN-level optimizations.
bullets: Convergent Encryption (Proof-of-Ownership for Cross-User CAS): Cross-user SHA-256 deduplication is vulnerable to a 'confirmation-of-a-file' side-channel attack if a malicious client simply guesses a known SHA-256 hash without possessing the file bytes. Fix this either by scoping deduplication per-tenant/workspace or by requiring clients to encrypt each chunk using a key derived from the chunk's own plaintext hash (Convergent Encryption / Message-Locked Encryption) plus a server challenge over random byte offsets.

Hot/Warm/Cold Storage Lifecycle Tiering: Newly uploaded CAS blocks start in S3 Standard. A background lifecycle policy transitions blocks untouched for 30 days to S3 Standard-IA, and blocks untouched for 90 days to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, cutting storage costs by 65% with millisecond retrieval.

Reference Counting & Orphan Block Garbage Collection: Because multiple file revisions can reference the same `block_hash`, blocks are never deleted synchronously on file deletion. A daily Spark/Flink mark-and-sweep job purges unreferenced staging blocks older than 24 hours and decrements `ref_count` on expired historical revisions.

LAN Sync Peer-to-Peer Transfer: When 50 employees in the same corporate office sync a shared 2 GB video folder, downloading 50× from S3 saturates the office WAN link. Desktop clients broadcast local chunk availability via UDP multicast on the local subnet and fetch verified `SHA-256` blocks directly from peer LAN devices.

tradeOffs.option: Fixed-Size Block Chunking (e.g., strict 4 MB offsets)
tradeOffs.pros: Trivial to compute on the client using simple byte-offset arithmetic; zero CPU overhead for rolling hash calculation.
tradeOffs.cons: Inserting a single byte at the beginning of a file shifts all subsequent chunk boundaries, invalidating 100% of downstream chunks and destroying delta sync efficiency.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Append-only log files, immutable video segments, or simple backup blobs that are never edited in place.

tradeOffs.option: Content-Defined Chunking (Rabin Fingerprinting)
tradeOffs.pros: Chunk boundaries depend strictly on local byte content; mid-file insertions or deletions only affect the single modified chunk while all subsequent chunks deduplicate cleanly.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher client CPU usage to compute rolling hashes and requires tracking variable chunk lengths in the metadata manifest.
tradeOffs.bestFor: General-purpose cloud drives (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive) handling editable documents, archives, and media.

tradeOffs.option: Proxy Upload through App Servers vs. Direct Presigned S3 Upload
tradeOffs.pros: Direct Presigned S3 Upload offloads hundreds of Gbps of binary throughput from application servers and routes clients to the nearest cloud edge POP.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires a two-phase Metadata Init -> S3 Upload -> Metadata Commit protocol with asynchronous S3 event verification.
tradeOffs.bestFor: All high-scale file and media storage architectures.

subtopics.interviewTip: Interviewers love testing whether you understand why fixed-size chunking fails when editing the start of a file. Explicitly explain **Content-Defined Chunking (Rabin rolling hash)** and pair it with the **two-step Init/Precheck -> Presigned Upload -> OCC Commit** flow so the interviewer sees both bandwidth deduplication and metadata consistency.

subtopics.title: Payment System
subtopics.subtitle: Stripe / PayPal Architecture: Idempotency Keys, Double-Entry Ledger, PSP Orchestration & T+1 Settlement Reconciliation
keyTakeaways: Enforce end-to-end idempotency at every layer: clients pass a UUID `Idempotency-Key` locked atomically in Redis/DB (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`), and the Payment Executor passes a deterministic `payment_order_id` to external PSPs so network retries never double-charge a card.

Model every cent of movement using an immutable, append-only Double-Entry Ledger where every transaction writes at least two balanced rows (`SUM(debits) == SUM(credits)`), never using `UPDATE account SET balance = balance - X` as the sole record.

Never hold a database transaction open across an external HTTP call to a PSP (Visa/Mastercard/Stripe): persist state `EXECUTING` first, call the PSP outside the DB transaction, and transition to `CAPTURED` or `FAILED` via a state machine + Transactional Outbox.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A Payment System (like Stripe, Adyen, or Uber/Amazon's internal payment platform) processes pay-ins from buyers and pay-outs to merchants across credit cards, bank transfers (ACH/SEPA), and digital wallets with zero financial discrepancy.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Pay-In flow: Authorize and capture funds from a buyer's payment instrument for a checkout session containing one or more merchant sub-orders; (2) Pay-Out flow: Disburse settled balances to merchant bank accounts; (3) Refund & Void support (full or partial); (4) Immutable Double-Entry Ledger recording every movement across buyer, platform escrow, PSP fee, and merchant accounts; (5) Automated T+1 Settlement Reconciliation against external PSP/bank settlement files.

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Consistency: Strict serializable ACID consistency for payment state transitions and ledger entries—zero lost, duplicated, or phantom transactions; (2) Reliability & Durability: 99.999% availability on the payment acceptance path; (3) Latency: P99 < 500ms for internal orchestration (excluding external bank/3DS network latency which takes 1–3s); (4) Security & Compliance: PCI-DSS Level 1 isolation (raw PAN card numbers are tokenized in a dedicated Card Vault and never touch core payment services).
Out of Scope: Issuing physical credit cards, consumer BNPL credit underwriting models, and cryptocurrency blockchain settlement.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: Unlike social media feeds with millions of QPS, payment systems have moderate QPS where every single request carries high financial value and strict transactional overhead.
bullets: Transaction Volume: 100 Million payment transactions per day (~$5 Billion daily GMV).
Average & Peak Write QPS: 100M / 86,400 sec ≈ 1,157 payment transactions/sec average. During Black Friday / Cyber Monday or flash sales (10x peak spike) -> ~12,000 payment transactions/sec.

Ledger Amplification: Each payment transaction generates 1 `PaymentEvent`, 1–2 `PaymentOrder` rows, and 4 immutable `LedgerEntry` rows (Buyer Debit, Platform Receivable Credit, Platform Payable Debit, Merchant Credit) -> ~60,000 DB row inserts/sec at peak.
Read Traffic: 500 Million status checks, merchant dashboard queries, and webhook deliveries per day (~5,800 reads/sec avg, ~30,000 reads/sec peak).
Average Record Size: `PaymentEvent` + `PaymentOrder` + `IdempotencyRecord` ≈ 2 KB; 4 `LedgerEntry` rows ≈ 1 KB total; Audit & Risk snapshot = 2 KB -> ~5 KB per transaction.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Financial regulations require retaining transaction and ledger records for 7 to 10 years, making immutable storage and fast idempotency caching key capacity dimensions.
bullets: Write QPS: 1,157 TPS average; 12,000 TPS peak (Black Friday). Database IOPS at peak ≈ 12,000 TPS × 6 rows = 72,000 write IOPS.
Read QPS: 5,800 QPS average; 30,000 QPS peak.

Redis Memory (Idempotency Locks & Hot Account Balances): (a) Idempotency keys cached in Redis with 48-hour TTL: 200M transactions × 256 bytes = 51.2 GB; (b) Active Merchant Wallet/Balance cache for 10M merchants × 256 bytes = 2.56 GB. With 2x replication + overhead, a 128 GB Redis cluster is more than sufficient.

5-Year Relational & Ledger Storage: 100M transactions/day × 5 KB = 500 GB/day -> 182.5 TB/year -> 912.5 TB raw over 5 years. With 3-way synchronous Raft replication (CockroachDB / Spanner / Aurora Multi-AZ) and B-Tree indexes (1.4x) -> 912.5 TB × 3 × 1.4 = 3.83 PB.
Bandwidth: Peak Ingress/Egress = (12,000 writes + 30,000 reads) × 4 KB = 168 MB/sec (1.34 Gbps).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The payment architecture isolates synchronous checkout acceptance from downstream wallet updates, double-entry ledger bookkeeping, and T+1 bank settlement reconciliation.
bullets: Payment Orchestrator & Idempotency Layer: Validates the request's `Idempotency-Key` using an atomic database/Redis lock, persists the `PaymentEvent` and `PaymentOrder`, and coordinates the state machine.
Risk & Fraud Engine: Evaluates device fingerprint, velocity rules, and ML fraud scores synchronously in <40ms before contacting external card networks.

PSP Connector & Dynamic Router: Routes the charge to Stripe, Adyen, or Braintree based on currency, card BIN acceptance rates, and real-time PSP health metrics, passing `paymentOrderId` as the external idempotency key.

Wallet Service & Double-Entry Ledger Service: Triggered via Kafka (fed by a Debezium CDC / Transactional Outbox on `payment_orders`). Credits the seller's payable balance and writes balanced Debit/Credit rows to `ledger_entries`.

Reconciliation Engine: Nightly batch pipeline that ingests CSV/ISO-20022 settlement files from PSPs, joins them with internal `ledger_entries` by `payment_order_id`, and routes any mismatches to an exception queue.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: We examine the two most critical payment engineering flows: (Flow 1) End-to-End Idempotent Payment Execution without holding DB locks over network calls, and (Flow 2) Double-Entry Ledger Posting & T+1 Settlement Reconciliation.
bullets: Flow 1 — Idempotent Execution & Two-Phase State Transition: A cardinal sin in payment systems is opening a `@Transactional` DB connection, calling `stripeClient.charge()` inside it (which can hang for 3 seconds), and committing afterward—this exhausts the DB connection pool in seconds during a PSP brownout. Instead: (Step 1) In short DB Transaction 1, insert the `idempotency_keys` record and `payment_orders` row in state `EXECUTING` and commit immediately. (Step 2) Outside any DB transaction, call the PSP passing `paymentOrderId` as the PSP's idempotency key. If the network times out, retry with Exponential Backoff + Jitter using the *same* `paymentOrderId`. (Step 3) In short DB Transaction 2, transition the order `EXECUTING -> CAPTURED` and write an `outbox_events` row in the same ACID commit.

Flow 2 — Double-Entry Accounting & T+1 Reconciliation: Consuming the `PaymentCaptured` event from Kafka, the Ledger Service records 4 balanced entries within a single transaction (e.g., for a $100.00 charge with a $3.00 platform fee: Debit `BUYER_EXTERNAL_CLEARING` $100.00; Credit `PLATFORM_CASH` $100.00; Debit `PLATFORM_ESCROW` $97.00 + `PLATFORM_REVENUE` $3.00; Credit `MERCHANT_PAYABLE` $97.00). At midnight (T+1), the Reconciliation Engine streams the PSP's settlement report and compares `(payment_order_id, captured_amount_cents)` against the internal ledger, classifying discrepancies into (a) Missing in Internal DB, (b) Missing in PSP Settlement, or (c) Amount Mismatch.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: At Tier-1 financial institutions and global payment processors, production readiness centers on multi-PSP failover, hot-account sharding, and regulatory isolation.
bullets: Hot Ledger Account Sharding (Sub-Accounts): The platform's central `ACCT_PSP_RECEIVABLE` and `ACCT_PLATFORM_FEE_REVENUE` accounts are updated on *every* transaction (12,000 TPS at peak). If updating a single `ledger_accounts` balance row acquires a row-level lock, PostgreSQL/CockroachDB will suffer severe lock contention (~500 TPS limit per row). Shard hot system accounts into `N = 64` sub-accounts (`ACCT_PSP_RECEIVABLE#00` .. `#63`) hashed by `payment_order_id`, and sum across the 64 shards when reading the total balance.

Dynamic Multi-PSP Smart Routing & Circuit Breaking: Monitor rolling 60-second authorization success rates and P99 latencies per PSP (Stripe, Adyen, Worldpay) segmented by country and card network. If Stripe's European gateway experiences a brownout, a Resilience4j circuit breaker automatically reroutes traffic to Adyen using the universal Card Vault token.

PCI-DSS Vault Isolation (Zero PAN in Core Scope): The frontend collects raw 16-digit PAN card numbers inside an isolated iframe hosted directly by a PCI-hardened Card Vault Service, returning an opaque `tok_xxx` token. Core microservices never see or log raw card numbers, shrinking PCI audit scope by 90%.

Dangling `EXECUTING` Order Sweeper: If a Payment Orchestrator pod crashes in the middle of Step 2 (while waiting for the PSP HTTP response) and the PSP webhook is delayed, a background Sweeper job queries orders stuck in `EXECUTING` for `> 60 seconds` and polls the PSP's `GET /v1/charges?idempotency_key={paymentOrderId}` endpoint to converge the state.

tradeOffs.option: Single Balance Column (`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + X`) vs. Double-Entry Ledger
tradeOffs.pros: Single column update is simple to implement and uses 4x less storage.
tradeOffs.cons: Impossible to audit how a balance was derived; if a bug corrupts the number, there is no immutable trail of where the money came from or went.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Non-financial loyalty points or gaming coins; NEVER acceptable for real-money payment systems.

tradeOffs.option: Synchronous Ledger Write on Checkout Path vs. Asynchronous Outbox + Kafka Ledger Write
tradeOffs.pros: Asynchronous Outbox keeps checkout latency fast and isolates the buyer from downstream reporting/wallet shard contention.
tradeOffs.cons: Merchant dashboard balance shows eventual consistency (typically 100–500ms lag after payment capture).
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput payment platforms (Stripe, Uber, Amazon) where buyer checkout speed and 99.999% availability are paramount.

tradeOffs.option: Single PSP Integration vs. Multi-PSP Orchestration with Card Vault
tradeOffs.pros: Multi-PSP orchestration prevents single-vendor outages and improves global card authorization rates by 2–4% via local acquiring.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires building and certifying an internal PCI-DSS Level 1 Card Vault and normalizing heterogeneous PSP webhook formats.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Global enterprises processing >$1B/year in GMV.

subtopics.interviewTip: Always highlight two non-negotiable rules early in a Payment System interview: (1) **Never use `float` or `double`**—use integer `long amountCents` + `currency` (or `BigDecimal`), and (2) **Never hold a database transaction open while calling an external PSP over HTTP**—use a two-step state transition (`INITIALIZED -> EXECUTING` committed before HTTP, then `EXECUTING -> CAPTURED` + Outbox committed after HTTP).

subtopics.title: Ticket Booking
subtopics.subtitle: Ticketmaster / BookMyShow Architecture: Virtual Waiting Room, Temporary Seat Holds, OCC & Flash-Sale Stampede Defense
keyTakeaways: Prevent double-booking using a Two-Phase Seat Reservation pattern: Phase 1 acquires an atomic 10-minute temporary hold (`AVAILABLE -> HELD`) using Redis Lua / DB Optimistic Concurrency Control (`version` check), and Phase 2 transitions `HELD -> BOOKED` upon payment completion.

Protect the core booking database during celebrity concert drops (e.g., Taylor Swift / Coldplay with 5M concurrent fans for 50,000 seats) using an Edge Virtual Waiting Room (Queue-it style token bucket) that admits users into the seat-map checkout at a controlled rate.

Never rely solely on a Redis TTL expiration event to release abandoned holds: store `hold_expires_at` directly in the database seat row so any query or CAS update treats an expired `HELD` seat (`hold_expires_at < NOW()`) as immediately bookable.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A Ticket Booking platform (like Ticketmaster, BookMyShow, or StubHub) sells assigned seats for concerts, sports games, and movie screenings. The defining challenge is surviving extreme flash-sale traffic spikes while guaranteeing zero double-booked seats.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Users can browse events, venues, and real-time interactive seat maps (`AVAILABLE`, `HELD`, `BOOKED`); (2) Users can select up to 6 specific seats (or request 'Best Available' contiguous seats) and lock them for a 10-minute checkout window; (3) If payment succeeds within 10 minutes, the seats transition to `BOOKED` and an e-ticket QR code is issued; (4) If payment fails or the 10-minute timer expires, the seats automatically return to `AVAILABLE`; (5) Fair admission during high-demand drops via a Virtual Waiting Room.

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Consistency: Strict strong consistency on seat reservations—**zero double booking** under any concurrency scenario; (2) Availability: 99.99% for event browsing and waiting room admission; (3) Latency: P99 < 100ms for loading the venue seat map, P99 < 200ms for acquiring a seat hold; (4) Surge Isolation: A flash sale on 1 hot concert must not degrade movie ticket bookings across the rest of the platform.
Out of Scope: Secondary peer-to-peer ticket resale marketplace, dynamic airline yield pricing algorithms, and venue turnstile hardware firmware.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: Normal daily traffic is modest, but flash sales create a 100x–500x hotspot on a single `show_id` within a 60-second window.
bullets: Platform Baseline: 50 Million DAU browsing events; 3 Million tickets booked per day across 100,000 active shows (movies, concerts, sports).
Seat Inventory per Show: Movie theater = 300 seats; Arena concert = 20,000 seats; Stadium concert = 80,000 seats.
Flash Sale Hotspot Traffic: 5 Million concurrent users attempting to buy 80,000 seats for a single stadium concert at 10:00:00 AM.
Read Traffic: 500 Million seat-map views/day baseline (~5,800 QPS avg); during a flash sale, 5M users polling or connected via SSE = up to 500,000 seat-map reads/sec.

Write Traffic (Hold + Book): Baseline 3M bookings/day ≈ 35 bookings/sec; during a flash sale, the Virtual Waiting Room throttles active checkout admissions to 10,000 concurrent users -> ~5,000 seat-hold attempts/sec against the hot show.
Payload Sizes: Seat row in DB = 128 bytes; Compact Seat Map Status payload for an 80,000-seat stadium (2 bits per seat: `00`=Available, `01`=Held, `10`=Booked) = 20 KB compressed.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Because the total number of active seats across all upcoming shows is surprisingly small, the entire global seat inventory easily fits in memory!
bullets: Baseline & Flash-Sale Read QPS: 5,800 QPS average; 500,000 QPS peak during stadium drops (served via Edge CDN + Redis Bitfield/Hash cache).
Baseline & Flash-Sale Write QPS: 70 writes/sec average (Hold + Confirm); 10,000 writes/sec peak (throttled by Virtual Waiting Room pass verification).

Redis Memory (Active Show Seat Maps + Waiting Room Queues): (a) 100,000 active shows × average 2,000 seats × 64 bytes per seat in Redis = 12.8 GB! Even 1,000 stadium shows (80,000 seats each) take only 5.1 GB; (b) Virtual Waiting Room queues for 10M queued users × 64 bytes = 640 MB. A 64 GB Redis cluster holds every active seat on Earth in RAM.

5-Year Relational Storage (Bookings, Tickets & Historical Shows): 100,000 shows/day × 2,000 seats × 128 bytes = 25.6 GB/day + 3M bookings/day × 1 KB = 3 GB/day -> ~28.6 GB/day -> 10.4 TB/year -> 52.2 TB over 5 years. With 3x replication and indexes ≈ 200 TB.

Bandwidth: Peak Egress during flash sale = 500,000 seat-map reads/sec × 20 KB (compact bitfield/section JSON) = 10 GB/sec (80 Gbps, 95% offloaded by 1-second micro-caching at CDN/Edge + WebSocket delta pushes).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture uses a two-layer defense: an Edge Virtual Waiting Room to shape incoming flash-sale traffic, and a Redis + PostgreSQL/CockroachDB core partitioned by `show_id` to guarantee atomic multi-seat holds.
bullets: Edge Virtual Waiting Room (Cloudflare Workers + Redis ZSET): When a hot concert goes on sale, users join a virtual waiting room. At 10:00 AM, users are assigned a randomized queue position and popped in batches of 2,000/sec. Admitted users receive an HMAC-signed JWT `X-Queue-Pass-Token` valid for 15 minutes.

Seat Map Query Service & Compact Bitmap Cache: Serves the 80,000-seat stadium map from Redis and pushes real-time seat status diffs (`seatId: HELD`) over WebSockets/SSE to users currently viewing that stadium section.

Booking Service: Validates the `X-Queue-Pass-Token`, executes an atomic multi-seat hold in Redis via a Lua script (fast-fail gatekeeper), and commits the authoritative `AVAILABLE -> HELD` state transition in the relational database using OCC (`version` + lazy `hold_expires_at` check).

Hold Expiration Sweeper & Payment Webhook Listener: Confirms `HELD -> BOOKED` upon payment capture, or sweeps expired `HELD` rows (`hold_expires_at < NOW()`) back to `AVAILABLE` and updates the Redis bitmap.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Below we trace (Flow 1) Two-Phase Atomic Multi-Seat Hold with Lazy Expiration and OCC, and (Flow 2) Virtual Waiting Room Queue Admission & Contiguous 'Best Available' Seat Allocation.
bullets: Flow 1 — Atomic Multi-Seat Hold with Lazy Expiration & OCC: Suppose 1,000 users click seats `[101, 102]` at the exact same millisecond. First, a Redis Lua script checks if `seat:101` and `seat:102` are currently held; 999 requests fail in <0.5ms at the Redis layer without ever touching PostgreSQL. The 1 winning request proceeds to PostgreSQL, sorts the seat IDs `[101, 102]`, and executes an atomic update that succeeds *either* if `status = 'AVAILABLE'` *or* if `status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < NOW()` (Lazy Expiration!). This means even if a background cron job is delayed by 30 seconds, an expired seat hold is immediately bookable the exact millisecond `hold_expires_at` passes.

Flow 2 — Virtual Waiting Room & 'Best Available' Bitmask Search: For mega-events, showing a clickable 80,000-seat map causes severe contention because thousands of fans click the exact same front-row seats. Instead, the UI switches to 'Section / Best Available' mode: the user asks for `N = 4` contiguous seats in `Section 102`. The Booking Service represents each row of 32 seats as a 32-bit integer bitmask in memory (`0` = available, `1` = taken) and finds `N` adjacent available seats in $O(1)$ CPU cycles using bitwise shifts (`mask & (mask << 1) & (mask << 2) & (mask << 3)`).

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To survive extreme celebrity ticket drops and bot armies, production ticketing platforms add edge bot mitigation, anti-scalping cryptographic tickets, and dynamic UI degradation.
bullets: Lazy Expiration + Background Sweeper Dual Defense: Relying *only* on a background cron job to flip expired `HELD` rows back to `AVAILABLE` introduces a window where seats appear unavailable after 10 minutes if the cron lags. Relying *only* on lazy expiration leaves the Redis seat-map cache stale until someone clicks that seat. Combine both: the SQL `WHERE` clause checks `hold_expires_at < NOW()` for instant correctness, while a lightweight Sweeper every 5 seconds refreshes the Redis seat-map bitmap for the UI.

Dynamic UI Degradation (Interactive Seat Map -> Section Auto-Assign): When concurrent traffic for a single `show_id` exceeds 50,000 users, disable individual seat clicking on the frontend (which causes 99% OCC collisions on the most popular front-row seats) and switch to 'Select Section & Quantity' mode backed by per-section partitioned queues and bitwise contiguous seat allocation.

Anti-Scalper Bot Defense & Verified Fan Tokens: Require pre-registered 'Verified Fan' cryptographic tokens before entering the Virtual Waiting Room, combined with proof-of-work challenges and device attestation at the CDN edge so headless scripts cannot exhaust the 10-minute seat hold pool.

Rotating TOTP Dynamic QR Codes for Venue Entry: Static PDF barcodes are easily screenshotted and resold to multiple buyers. Issue tickets as a seed secret inside the mobile app that renders a rotating 15-second TOTP barcode (`HMAC-SHA256(ticketSecret, currentEpoch / 15)`), eliminating screenshot fraud at the stadium gates.

tradeOffs.option: Pessimistic Locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) vs. Optimistic Concurrency Control (`version` column)
tradeOffs.pros: Pessimistic locking serializes conflicting transactions inside the DB engine without throwing immediate retry errors.
tradeOffs.cons: Under a flash sale where 5,000 users target the same seat row, waiting on row locks ties up all database connections and causes cascading thread-pool exhaustion.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-contention back-office updates; for high-contention ticket drops, Redis fast-fail gatekeeping + DB OCC (`version` check) is far more resilient.

tradeOffs.option: Interactive Seat Map Selection vs. Server-Assigned 'Best Available' Section Allocation
tradeOffs.pros: Interactive Seat Map gives users exact control over aisle/view preferences.
tradeOffs.cons: Causes extreme collision rates during flash sales because thousands of users click the exact same visually prominent seats simultaneously.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Use Interactive Seat Map for movies and regular concerts; dynamically switch to 'Best Available' Section Allocation during stadium flash sales.

tradeOffs.option: Redis-Only Seat Hold vs. Redis Gatekeeper + Durable DB `hold_expires_at`
tradeOffs.pros: Redis-only holds are ultra-fast and expire automatically via Redis TTL.
tradeOffs.cons: If a Redis master crashes before replicating to its replica, two users can hold the same seat and both proceed to payment.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Always pair the Redis Lua gatekeeper with an authoritative ACID database update (`status = 'HELD'`, `hold_expires_at`) before initiating payment.

subtopics.interviewTip: Be sure to mention **Lazy Expiration** (`WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < NOW())`) and **sorting `seatIds` ascending** before locking multiple seats. Those two details immediately signal to the interviewer that you have built real concurrent reservation systems and know how to prevent both cron-lag unavailability and multi-row deadlocks.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: An E-commerce Order System (like Amazon, Flipkart, or Shopify Checkout) converts a buyer's shopping cart into a confirmed, paid, and warehouse-routed order while guaranteeing zero overselling and complete auditability across distributed microservices.
bullets: Functional Requirements: (1) Cart-to-Checkout validation: verify item availability, compute item-level tax & shipping, and validate coupon/promo rules; (2) Order creation with immutable price/tax/catalog snapshotting; (3) Atomic inventory reservation with automatic release if payment fails or times out; (4) Distributed checkout orchestration across Inventory, Payment, Promo, and Warehouse Fulfillment services; (5) Order lifecycle tracking (`PENDING_RESERVATION -> RESERVED -> PAID -> FULFILLING -> SHIPPED -> DELIVERED / CANCELLED`) and partial/full cancellations.

Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Consistency: Zero overselling of physical inventory and strict eventual consistency (via Saga) across Order, Inventory, and Payment states; (2) Availability: 99.99% on the order placement path; (3) Latency: P99 < 300ms for checkout initiation and inventory reservation; (4) Flash-Sale Resilience: Handle 50,000 concurrent checkout attempts on a single hot launch SKU without locking up the inventory database.
Out of Scope: Product search relevance ranking, recommendation engines, and last-mile delivery truck GPS routing.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the system for a global retail marketplace handling both steady daily shopping and massive Prime Day / Singles' Day flash peaks.
bullets: User Base & Order Volume: 300 Million MAU, 80 Million DAU; 25 Million completed orders per day baseline (averaging 3 line items per order = 75 Million `order_items` per day).
Peak Flash-Sale Multiplier: 15x traffic spike during Prime Day / Black Friday opening hour (~17,000 orders/sec across the platform).
Read-to-Write Ratio: 20:1 (buyers check order status, tracking pages, and order history 20 times for every 1 order placed -> 500 Million order reads/day).
Average Payload Sizes: `orders` header + 3 `order_items` (with immutable price/tax/product snapshot) + `saga_state_log` = 4 KB per order.
Catalog & SKU Footprint: 500 Million active SKUs across 200 regional fulfillment centers.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: We compute baseline and flash-sale QPS, Redis memory for hot SKU inventory counters and active carts, and 5-year sharded order database storage.
bullets: Order Write QPS: 25M orders / 86,400 sec ≈ 290 orders/sec average (~870 `order_items`/sec); Peak Order Write QPS (15x) ≈ 4,350 orders/sec (and up to 15,000 checkout attempts/sec including failed flash-sale attempts).
Order Read QPS: 500M reads / 86,400 sec ≈ 5,787 reads/sec average; Peak Read QPS (15x) ≈ 86,800 reads/sec.

Redis Memory (Active Shopping Carts + Hot SKU Inventory Tokens + Idempotency): (a) 80M DAU active carts × 2 KB = 160 GB; (b) 50M active/hot SKUs cached in Redis (`sku:{id}:stock` + reservation hashes) × 256 bytes = 12.8 GB; (c) 50M checkout idempotency keys (48h TTL) × 256 bytes = 12.8 GB. Total Redis RAM with 2x replication ≈ 372 GB.

5-Year Relational Storage (Orders + Order Items + Saga Audit Log): 25M orders/day × 4 KB = 100 GB/day -> 36.5 TB/year -> 182.5 TB raw over 5 years. With 3x replication and secondary indexes (`buyer_id`, `seller_id`, `created_at`) ≈ 766 TB across sharded PostgreSQL/Vitess/CockroachDB.
Bandwidth: Peak Ingress = 15,000 checkout QPS × 4 KB = 60 MB/sec (480 Mbps); Peak Egress = 86,800 read QPS × 4 KB = 347 MB/sec (2.78 Gbps).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The E-commerce Order architecture centers on a stateful Saga Orchestrator backed by the Transactional Outbox pattern, coordinating Inventory, Payment, and Warehouse Fulfillment over Kafka.
bullets: Checkout & Order Service (Saga Orchestrator): Snapshots current pricing/tax rules from the Cart & Pricing Service, writes the `orders`, `order_items`, `saga_instances`, and `outbox_events` rows in a single local ACID transaction, and drives the multi-step checkout workflow.

Inventory Service (Redis Token Gate + 64-Way Striped DB): Handles `ReserveInventoryCommand`. First checks/decrements the SKU's Redis token counter via Lua; if successful, persists the reservation in `sku_inventory_buckets` (`bucket_id = hash(orderId) % 64`) with a 15-minute payment TTL.
Payment Service: Processes `ProcessPaymentCommand` idempotently using `orderId` as the payment key. If the card is declined or expires after 15 minutes, emits `PaymentFailedEvent`.

Compensating Transaction Handler: When `PaymentFailedEvent` arrives, the Saga Orchestrator transitions the saga to `COMPENSATE_RELEASE_INVENTORY` and sends `ReleaseInventoryCommand` to restore the reserved stock back to the exact `bucket_id`.

Fulfillment & Order Split Service: Once paid, splits multi-item orders into physical `ShipmentOrder`s grouped by optimal fulfillment center proximity and dispatches pick-pack-ship tasks to the Warehouse Management System (WMS).

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: We detail the two most frequently probed deep-dive areas in an E-commerce interview: (Flow 1) Orchestrated Checkout Saga with Forward & Compensating Rollback Paths, and (Flow 2) High-Concurrency Flash-Sale Inventory Reservation via Redis Lua + 64-Way Database Bucketing.
bullets: Flow 1 — Orchestrated Checkout Saga & Compensating Rollback: Why Orchestration instead of Choreography for checkout? Because checkout has a clear central coordinator (the Order), and cyclic dependencies between Inventory, Payment, Promo Coupons, and Loyalty Points become a debugging nightmare in pure pub/sub choreography. In the Happy Path: `OrderCreated -> ReserveInventoryCmd -> InventoryReservedEvt -> ProcessPaymentCmd -> PaymentCapturedEvt -> ScheduleFulfillmentCmd -> OrderConfirmed`. In the Failure/Rollback Path: if `PaymentFailedEvt` arrives (or the 15-minute payment window expires), the Saga Orchestrator emits `ReleaseInventoryCmd` (and `RevokePromoRedemptionCmd`), waits for `InventoryReleasedEvt` ack, and marks the order `CANCELLED_PAYMENT_FAILED`.

Flow 2 — Striped Inventory Bucketing + Redis Lua Gatekeeper: A single PostgreSQL row `UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE sku_id = 'IPHONE_17' AND available >= 1` can only execute ~500 serializable updates/sec due to row-level lock contention. When 50,000 buyers click 'Buy Now' at 12:00:00 PM: (1) A Redis Lua script atomically checks and decrements `sku:IPHONE_17:available`, rejecting 49,000 excess buyers in sub-millisecond time once stock hits 0; (2) For the winning buyers, the Inventory Service hashes `orderId` into one of `64` database sub-rows (`bucket_id = Math.floorMod(orderId.hashCode(), 64)`), multiplying database write throughput by 64x (~32,000 reservations/sec).

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: Scaling an E-commerce Order System to support millions of third-party sellers and global fulfillment requires dual-sharded projections, bucket rebalancing, and asynchronous tax/fraud pipelines.
bullets: Tail-End Bucket Consolidation for Striped Inventory: When a flash-sale SKU has only 20 units left spread across 64 buckets (e.g., 1 unit in 20 different buckets) and a buyer orders `quantity = 2`, a single-bucket check would fail. Once total Redis remaining stock drops below `2 × NUM_INVENTORY_BUCKETS` (128 units), a lightweight background worker consolidates remaining stock into `bucket_id = 0` so multi-unit orders can still succeed cleanly.

Buyer vs. Seller Dual-Sharded Views (CQRS): Buyers query `GET /orders?buyerId=X` while third-party merchants query `GET /seller/orders?sellerId=Y`. Because a single buyer order can contain items from 3 different sellers, shard the authoritative `orders` table by `buyer_id` (or `order_id`), and stream `OrderItemCreated` events via Kafka into a read-optimized `seller_order_items` table sharded by `seller_id`.

Warehouse Geo-Routing & Order Splitting: If a buyer in Chicago orders 3 items where 2 are in the Illinois fulfillment center and 1 is only available in California, the Fulfillment Service splits the parent `Order` into two child `Shipment` entities after payment capture, minimizing shipping cost and delivery latency.

Abandoned Reservation Reaper: If a buyer reserves inventory at checkout and closes their browser tab without submitting payment, a background Reaper sweeps `inventory_reservations WHERE status = 'RESERVED' AND expires_at < NOW()`, emits `PAYMENT_TIMED_OUT` to the Saga Orchestrator, and restores both the DB bucket stock and Redis token counter.

tradeOffs.option: Saga Orchestration (Central Order Coordinator) vs. Saga Choreography (Peer-to-Peer Events)
tradeOffs.pros: Orchestration centralizes checkout state transitions and compensating rollbacks in one place (`saga_instances`), making timeout handling and debugging straightforward.
tradeOffs.cons: The Order Service must know the command contracts of Inventory, Payment, and Fulfillment services.
tradeOffs.bestFor: E-commerce checkout flows where a multi-step transaction has a clear owner (the Order) and strict rollback ordering.

tradeOffs.option: Reserve Inventory Before Payment vs. Deduct Inventory Only After Payment Capture
tradeOffs.pros: Reserving inventory *before* charging the buyer guarantees you never take a customer's money for an out-of-stock item (zero overselling refunds).
tradeOffs.cons: Requires a 10–15 minute reservation hold TTL and compensating release logic if the buyer abandons payment.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Flash sales, limited-stock physical goods, and high-trust retail marketplaces.

tradeOffs.option: Single SKU Row vs. 64-Way Striped Inventory Buckets
tradeOffs.pros: 64-way striped buckets eliminate database row-lock contention on hot SKUs, increasing single-SKU checkout throughput from ~500 TPS to >30,000 TPS.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires bucket probing or tail-end consolidation when remaining inventory is very low.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Platforms running flash sales, product drops, or high-velocity promotions (Amazon Prime Day, Flipkart Big Billion Days).

subtopics.interviewTip: When designing an E-commerce Order System, always emphasize two architectural pillars: (1) **Immutable Price & Tax Snapshotting** inside `order_items` (never join `order_items` with the live `products` table to calculate historical order totals!), and (2) **Saga Orchestration with 64-Way Striped Inventory Buckets** so flash-sale SKUs never bottleneck on a single database row lock.

subtopics.title: Uber / Ride Matching
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a real-time geospatial ride-dispatch engine with H3 hexagonal indexing, ETA calculation, and transactional driver locking
keyTakeaways: Partition the world into Uber H3 hexagonal cells (Resolution 8 ~ 0.73 km², Resolution 9 ~ 0.1 km²) where all 6 neighbors are equidistant, eliminating edge distortion at high latitudes.
Separate high-frequency ephemeral driver location pings (in-memory Redis Geo/H3 Cluster) from durable trip state machines (PostgreSQL/CockroachDB with optimistic locking).

Rank candidate drivers by actual road-network ETA (Dijkstra/Contraction Hierarchies with live traffic weights) rather than Euclidean Haversine distance, and use a distributed Redis lock (`SET NX EX 15`) during sequential/batched dispatch offers.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A global ride-hailing platform must continuously ingest millions of GPS telemetry pings from active drivers while matching riders to optimal nearby drivers with low latency and zero double-booking.
bullets: Functional — Driver Location Telemetry: Active drivers stream GPS coordinates (latitude, longitude, bearing, speed) every 4 seconds.
Functional — Fare & ETA Estimation: Riders enter pickup and drop-off coordinates to receive an upfront fare quote, route polyline, and estimated pickup time.

Functional — Real-Time Ride Matching: Upon ride confirmation, the system locates available drivers near the pickup cell, ranks them by road-network ETA, and dispatches an offer with a 12-second acceptance window.

Functional — Trip Lifecycle State Machine: Track state transitions (`REQUESTED` -> `OFFERED` -> `ACCEPTED` -> `ARRIVED` -> `IN_PROGRESS` -> `COMPLETED` / `CANCELLED`) and broadcast live driver location to the matched rider.
Non-Functional — Low Dispatch Latency: P99 location update ingestion < 100 ms; P99 rider-to-driver matching decision < 1.5 seconds.

Non-Functional — High Availability & Consistency: 99.99% availability for location tracking and dispatch; strict serializability on driver assignment (one driver cannot be matched to two riders simultaneously, and one trip cannot have two drivers).
Out of Scope: Driver onboarding/background checks, split-fare social payments, autonomous vehicle fleet telemetry, and food delivery multi-stop batching.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the system for a global ride-hailing deployment comparable to Uber across 10,000+ cities.
bullets: Daily Active Users (DAU): 40 Million Riders DAU and 6 Million Active Drivers DAU (with 1.5 Million concurrent online drivers at global peak).
Completed Trips per Day: 30 Million trips/day (plus ~10 Million fare estimate queries that do not convert, totaling 40M quote requests/day).
Driver Location Ping Frequency: Every online driver sends 1 ping every 4 seconds via persistent WebSocket/gRPC stream.
Read:Write Ratio: Location pipeline is write-heavy (~10:1 writes to dispatch reads), whereas rider map viewport radar and ETA polling generate ~3:1 reads to writes.
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 3x average traffic during Friday evening rush hour or major city events/rainstorms.
Payload Sizes: Driver GPS ping payload = 128 bytes (JSON/Protobuf); Redis H3 driver state entry = 256 bytes; Trip relational record = 1.5 KB; Route breadcrumb point = 64 bytes.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: The dominant workload is the continuous firehose of GPS location pings from 1.5 million concurrent drivers, which must be absorbed in memory without thrashing disk-backed relational databases.
bullets: Location Write QPS: 1.5M concurrent online drivers / 4 seconds = 375,000 writes/sec average active rate, bursting to 1,125,000 writes/sec at 3x regional surge.
Ride Match & Quote QPS: 40M quotes/day / 86,400s = ~463 QPS average (1,400 Peak QPS); 30M trips/day / 86,400s = ~347 Ride Creation QPS average (~1,050 Peak QPS).

Redis Geo-Index Memory (RAM): 6M active drivers * 256 bytes + H3 cell sets & hash overhead (~512 bytes/driver total) = ~3.1 GB raw -> provisioned across a 64 GB Redis Cluster (16 shards, master-replica) for CPU/PPS headroom rather than RAM capacity.

5-Year Storage (Trips + GPS Breadcrumbs): 30M trips/day * 1.5 KB = 45 GB/day (~82 TB over 5 years). GPS Breadcrumbs (sampled every 12s for active trips: 750K concurrent in-trip drivers / 12s = 62,500 pts/sec * 64 B = 4 MB/sec = 345 GB/day -> 630 TB over 5 years, or ~1.89 PB with 3x replication in Cassandra/S3).

Ingress & Egress Bandwidth: Ingress = 375,000 pings/sec * 128 B = 48 MB/sec (144 MB/sec peak). Egress (rider map radar + active trip tracking for 1.5M riders every 4s * 512 B) = ~192 MB/sec average (576 MB/sec peak).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture splits into two distinct planes: the **High-Throughput Ephemeral Geo Plane** (handling 375K+ location pings/sec in memory using Uber H3 cells) and the **Transactional Trip & Dispatch Plane** (coordinating offers, distributed locks, and durable trip records).
bullets: Edge WebSocket / gRPC Gateway: Terminates TLS and maintains sticky bidirectional streams with millions of driver and rider mobile apps.

Location Ingestion Service & Redis H3 Cluster: Converts `(lat, lng)` into a 64-bit H3 index (`res=8`). Updates the driver's current position and maintains a Redis Set per H3 cell (`h3:cell:{h3Index}:drivers`) with a 15-second TTL to automatically evict disconnected drivers.

Routing & ETA Engine (OSRM / Contraction Hierarchies): Partitioned by metropolitan region. Computes turn-by-turn road-network travel time rather than straight-line distance (critical when rivers, highways, or one-way streets separate a driver and rider).

Dispatch Orchestrator: Queries `kRing(pickupH3, k=1..3)` from Redis, filters available drivers matching the requested `VehicleType`, ranks them by road ETA, and acquires an atomic per-driver lock before pushing an offer.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let us examine the two core critical paths: (1) Atomic H3 Cell Migration on Driver Location Ping, and (2) K-Ring Candidate Discovery with Distributed Driver Locking during Ride Matching.
bullets: Flow 1 (Atomic H3 Cell Update): When a driver moves across an H3 hexagon boundary, we cannot naively `SREM` the old cell and `SADD` the new cell in two separate network round-trips, or the driver could vanish or appear in two cells simultaneously. An atomic Redis Lua script compares the previous H3 cell stored in the driver's hash with the newly computed H3 cell, moves the driver ID between sets, and refreshes the 15-second heartbeat TTL.

Flow 2 (K-Ring Search & Offer Locking): When a rider requests a trip at `(pickupLat, pickupLng)`, the Dispatch Service computes `originH3 = h3.latLngToCell(lat, lng, 8)` and fetches all 7 cells in `gridDisk(originH3, 1)` (center + 6 equidistant neighbors). After filtering online drivers and ranking via the Routing Engine, the dispatcher attempts `SET lock:driver:{driverId} {tripId} NX EX 15`. Only the dispatcher thread that wins the lock sends the push notification to the driver; if the driver rejects or times out after 12 seconds, the lock is released and the next-best candidate is locked.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: Moving from single-rider greedy dispatch to a globally resilient production system requires batch optimization, surge feedback loops, and edge-case handling.
bullets: Global Bipartite Batch Matching (Hungarian / Min-Cost Max-Flow): Instead of greedily assigning the closest driver to the first request (which may steal a driver who is 1 minute away from Rider B to serve Rider A who is 5 minutes away), buffer requests over a 2-second window in dense H3 cells and solve a minimum-weight bipartite matching problem to minimize aggregate wait time across all riders.

Forward Dispatch (On-Trip Matching): Include drivers who are in `IN_PROGRESS` status and within 90 seconds of their current drop-off coordinate inside the drop-off H3 cell's candidate pool, dramatically increasing effective fleet utilization during rush hour.

Dead-Reckoning & Map Matching (Kalman Filters): Raw urban GPS bounces off skyscrapers (multipath interference). Snap incoming `(lat, lng, bearing)` points onto valid road segments using a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) before indexing into H3.

Hot-Cell Surge Protection (Airports & Stadiums): When an event ends at a stadium, a single H3 cell can receive 10,000 ride requests in 60 seconds. Use Virtual Queues (FIFO token buckets per pickup zone) and replicate hot H3 cell lookups across local L1 Caffeine caches with 1-second TTL.

Multi-Region Active-Active Sharding: Since riders in Tokyo never match with drivers in New York, shard both the Redis H3 Clusters and PostgreSQL Trip databases by Metropolitan Geo-Region (`city_id`), eliminating cross-continent distributed transactions.

tradeOffs.option: Uber H3 Hexagonal Hierarchical Index
tradeOffs.pros: All 6 neighboring cells have identical center-to-center distances; fast bit-shift parent/child resolution traversal; zero polar/meridian singularities for city regions.
tradeOffs.cons: Slight area variation (~1.6x max/min hexagon area ratio across the globe) and requires converting lat/lng via the H3 C/Java native library.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Ride-hailing dispatch, dynamic surge pricing heatmaps, and k-ring radius searches.

tradeOffs.option: Google S2 Geometry (Quadtree on Sphere)
tradeOffs.pros: Exact hierarchical containment (1 parent square = 4 child squares) and native range-scan prefix queries.
tradeOffs.cons: Squares have 4 edge neighbors and 4 diagonal neighbors at different distances (1 vs sqrt(2)), complicating uniform radial expansion.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Strict polygon containment queries and hierarchical storage prefix scans.

tradeOffs.option: Geohash (Base32 Z-Order Curve) / PostGIS R-Tree
tradeOffs.pros: Simple string prefix matching (`WHERE geohash LIKE '9q8yy%'`); built into standard Redis `GEOADD`.
tradeOffs.cons: Severe edge boundary cliff problem (two points 10 meters apart across the Prime Meridian or cell seam share zero prefix characters).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Simple store-locator apps with low update frequency.

subtopics.interviewTip: Interviewers immediately test two things in an Uber design: (1) Why H3 hexagons beat Geohashes/Quadtrees (all 6 neighbors share the exact same distance from the center cell, and dynamic surge pricing smoothing across rings is trivial), and (2) How you prevent two dispatch servers from assigning the same driver at the exact same millisecond (use `SET lock:driver:{id} {tripId} NX EX 15` in Redis before sending the offer push notification, backed by `@Version` optimistic locking on the `Trip` row).

subtopics.subtitle: Designing an ultra-low-latency electronic exchange & brokerage with LMAX Disruptor, deterministic single-threaded Limit Order Books, and Raft-replicated event journals
keyTakeaways: Never use database locks or multi-threaded mutexes inside a Limit Order Book (LOB): partition matching engines by `symbol` and run each symbol's order book on a single pinned CPU core using an LMAX Disruptor ring buffer.

Achieve fault tolerance via Deterministic State Machine Replication: sequence every command through a Raft-replicated append-only journal (Aeron Cluster / Chronicle Queue) so standby replicas reconstruct the exact same in-memory Order Book in microseconds.

Model price levels with a dual data structure: a `TreeMap<Long, PriceLevel>` (or flat array indexed by tick offset) for $O(1)$ best bid/ask lookup and doubly-linked lists of `OrderNode`s at each price level for $O(1)$ FIFO time-priority matching and $O(1)$ cancellation via `HashMap<Long, OrderNode>`.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: We are designing both the retail/institutional Order Management Gateway (brokerage pre-trade risk + wallet reservation) and the core Exchange Matching Engine that executes Limit and Market orders with strict price-time priority.
bullets: Functional — Order Placement & Cancellation: Support `LIMIT` and `MARKET` orders (`BUY` / `SELL`), Time-in-Force (`DAY`, `IOC`, `FOK`), and sub-millisecond order cancellations.

Functional — Pre-Trade Risk & Buying Power Validation: Synchronously verify sufficient cash balance (for buys) or share inventory/margin limits (for sells) and reserve funds before routing to the matching engine.

Functional — Price-Time Priority Matching (FIFO): Match incoming aggressive orders against resting orders in the Limit Order Book (LOB) strictly by best price first, then earliest arrival sequence number.
Functional — Real-Time Market Data Feeds: Broadcast Level-1 (Best Bid/Offer & Last Trade) and Level-2 (Order Book Depth across price levels) plus OHLCV candlestick bars (1s, 1m, 1h, 1d).

Non-Functional — Ultra-Low Deterministic Latency: Matching engine execution time < 50 microseconds P99 (sub-10 milliseconds end-to-end for retail REST gateways; < 500 microseconds for institutional FIX gateways).
Non-Functional — Strict Determinism & Zero Data Loss: 100% deterministic replayability from the sequenced command log; zero lost trades (`RPO = 0`) and automatic sub-second failover (`RTO < 200ms`).
Out of Scope: Multi-leg options/derivatives pricing models (Black-Scholes Greeks), T+1 regulatory tax reporting (1099-B generation), and dark pool midpoint pegging.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the system for a major US equity exchange and high-volume retail brokerage handling market-open and Fed-announcement volatility spikes.
bullets: Active Traders & Tradable Instruments: 15 Million DAU retail traders + 500 institutional market makers trading across 8,000 listed equity symbols (e.g., `AAPL`, `NVDA`, `TSLA`, `SPY`).

Order Events per Trading Day: 1.5 Billion total order events (New Order, Cancel, Modify) during a 6.5-hour trading session (23,400 seconds) — market makers generate ~10–15 cancellations/quotes per executed trade.
Executed Trades (Fills) per Day: 150 Million matched trades (300 Million ledger postings) per day.

Read:Write Ratio: Inside the matching engine, 100% of commands are sequenced state transitions; externally, 1 order book mutation triggers fan-out to tens of thousands of subscribed market-data WebSocket streams (~100:1 egress-to-ingress).
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 10x burst at 09:30:00 EST Market Open and 16:00:00 EST Market Close.
Payload Sizes: Binary SBE/FIX Order Command = 128 bytes; In-Memory Order Node = 128 bytes (cache-line aligned); Trade Execution Fill Event = 256 bytes; L2 Market Data Tick = 64 bytes.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Because the US trading day is concentrated into 23,400 seconds (6.5 hours) with extreme 10x spikes at the opening bell, QPS must be calculated against active market seconds rather than 86,400 seconds.
bullets: Order Ingress QPS: 1.5 Billion order events / 23,400s = ~64,100 orders/sec average -> 641,000 orders/sec at 10x Market Open peak.
Trade Execution QPS: 150 Million fills / 23,400s = ~6,410 trades/sec average -> 64,100 trades/sec at 10x peak.

Matching Engine Memory (RAM): 50 Million maximum concurrent resting open orders across all 8,000 symbols * 128 bytes = 6.4 GB raw in-memory LOB state + 15M active user risk/wallet accounts * 256 bytes = 3.84 GB -> easily fits inside L3 cache / 32 GB RAM per bare-metal node with zero swap or GC pauses.

5-Year Regulatory Audit & Ledger Storage (SEC Rule 17a-4): 1.5B order events/day * 128 B (192 GB/day) + 150M fills/day * 256 B (38.4 GB/day) = ~230.4 GB/trading day. At 252 trading days/year * 5 years = 1,260 trading days * 230.4 GB = ~290.3 TB raw -> ~871 TB with 3x replication.

Ingress & Market Data Egress Bandwidth: Ingress = 641,000 peak orders/sec * 128 B = 82 MB/sec peak. Egress (Market Data Multicast + WebSocket fan-out to 2M concurrent streaming clients receiving 20 updates/sec * 64 B) = 2.56 GB/sec (20.5 Gbps) at edge fan-out.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The system separates **Client Protocol Gateways** (FIX 4.2/SBE for institutions, REST/WebSocket for retail), the **Pre-Trade Risk Engine**, the **Deterministic Sequenced Matching Engine** (sharded by symbol range), and the asynchronous **Post-Trade Clearing & Market Data Pipeline**.
bullets: Order Gateways: Normalize REST JSON and institutional FIX messages into compact binary Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) structs.

Pre-Trade Risk Service: Sharded by `accountId`. Keeps user cash balances and share positions in memory (backed by a write-ahead log) to perform sub-millisecond buying power checks and reserve funds before an order ever reaches the exchange.

Sequencer & Raft Log (Aeron Cluster): Assigns a strictly monotonically increasing `sequenceNo` to every command and replicates it to a quorum of 3 nodes in memory-mapped files before the primary matching thread executes it.

Single-Threaded Matching Engine (LMAX Disruptor): Processes commands sequentially from the ring buffer with zero locks, zero context switches, and $O(1)$ price-level operations, emitting execution reports and market data ticks.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let us trace: (1) Pre-Trade Risk Reservation & Deterministic Sequenced Order Submission, and (2) The Single-Threaded Price-Time Priority Limit Order Book Matching & Cancellation Loop.
bullets: Flow 1 (Pre-Trade Reservation & Deterministic Replay): When a user places a Buy Limit Order for 100 shares of `AAPL` at `$200.00`, the Risk Engine atomically checks `availableCash >= $20,000` and moves `$20,000` into `reservedCash`. The command is appended to the symbol shard's Raft log with `seqNo = 984120`. If the order later fills at a better price (say `$199.50` via price improvement), the Post-Trade Execution handler releases the `$50.00` price improvement back to `availableCash`.

Flow 2 (In-Memory Limit Order Book Matching): The matching thread inspects the incoming order against the opposite side of the book. For a `BUY` order, it peeks `asks.firstEntry()`. As long as `bestAsk.priceCents <= buyOrder.priceCents` and `buyOrder.leavesQty > 0`, it walks the doubly-linked list of resting `OrderNode`s at `bestAsk` from `head` to `tail` (FIFO time priority). Filled resting nodes are unlinked in $O(1)$ and removed from `orderByIdMap` in $O(1)$. Any remaining `leavesQty` on the incoming limit order is appended to the tail of `bids.computeIfAbsent(buyPrice)`.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: Operating a regulated financial exchange requires mechanical sympathy, hardware optimization, and automated market-integrity safeguards.
bullets: Zero-GC Off-Heap Memory & Object Pooling: Replace standard `HashMap<Long, OrderNode>` and `TreeMap` with Agrona/Eclipse Collections primitive maps (`Long2ObjectHashMap`) and pre-allocate a slab of 10 Million `OrderNode` instances at JVM startup so Young/Old GC pauses are literally zero during trading hours.

Kernel Bypass Networking (DPDK / Solarflare OpenOnload) & CPU Pinning: Pin each matching engine thread to an isolated physical CPU core (`isolcpus`) with hyperthreading disabled, and read UDP multicast/Aeron IPC frames directly from the NIC ring buffer in user space.

Self-Trade Prevention (STP) & LULD Circuit Breakers: Prevent two orders from the same `accountId` or institutional firm from matching against each other (wash trading), and automatically pause matching for 5 minutes if a stock's price moves outside Limit-Up / Limit-Down (LULD) percentage bands within a rolling 5-minute window.

Fast Recovery via Memory-Mapped Snapshots + Raft Replay: Periodically snapshot the in-memory LOB from a warm follower node to disk every 5 minutes so a cold node restart only replays the last few minutes of the Chronicle/Aeron event log rather than the entire trading day.

Double-Entry Immutable Clearing Ledger: Every `MatchFill` event is consumed from Kafka into an append-only double-entry accounting ledger where `SUM(debits) == SUM(credits)` is enforced per transaction batch.

tradeOffs.option: Single-Threaded LMAX Disruptor + In-Memory LOB per Symbol Shard
tradeOffs.pros: Zero lock contention, zero context switching, CPU L1/L2 cache locality, 100% deterministic execution order, and > 1M orders/sec per core.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires careful symbol-to-shard assignment (hot tickers like NVDA/TSLA need dedicated single-symbol shards) and strict avoidance of any blocking I/O on the matching thread.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core stock/crypto exchange matching engines and pre-trade risk engines.

tradeOffs.option: Multi-Threaded Fine-Grained Locking Order Book
tradeOffs.pros: Allows multiple threads to mutate different price levels concurrently within the same symbol.
tradeOffs.cons: In real trading, 95%+ of activity hits the top 1–2 price levels (Best Bid/Ask), causing catastrophic mutex/CAS cache-line bouncing that makes multi-threading slower than a single thread.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Almost never recommended for high-frequency financial order books.

tradeOffs.option: Relational Database Row-Locking (`SELECT FOR UPDATE`)
tradeOffs.pros: Simple ACID transactions out of the box with zero custom replication logic.
tradeOffs.cons: Capped at ~1,000–2,000 TPS per symbol with 5–20 ms latency — orders of magnitude too slow for a live exchange.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-volume internal auction tools or end-of-day settlement batch processing.

subtopics.interviewTip: Always emphasize three golden rules in a Stock Trading interview: (1) Store prices as `long` integer cents or micro-dollars, never `double`/`float`; (2) Never use locks or database queries inside the matching loop — use a single-threaded LMAX Disruptor per symbol shard; and (3) Achieve `O(1)` order cancellation by combining a `HashMap<OrderId, OrderNode>` with a doubly-linked list inside each `PriceLevel`.

subtopics.subtitle: Designing a cloud-scale cron & delayed task execution engine with time-bucketed sharding, hierarchical timing wheels, and fencing-token leases
keyTakeaways: Partition schedule scanning by `(time_bucket_minute, shard_id)` so schedule Pollers perform sequential partition scans on the current minute window rather than expensive unindexed range queries across billions of future jobs.

Bridge the gap between minute-level DB buckets and sub-second execution accuracy using an in-memory Hierarchical Timing Wheel (`HashedWheelTimer`) before dispatching ready tasks to Kafka worker queues.

Guarantee safe execution under worker crashes using Lease Expirations (`visibility_timeout`), Heartbeat extensions, and monotonically increasing `fencing_token` numbers so zombie workers cannot corrupt downstream state.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A distributed job scheduler (like AWS EventBridge Scheduler, Google Cloud Tasks, or Temporal/Quartz at scale) allows thousands of internal microservices and external tenants to schedule one-off delayed tasks, recurring cron jobs, and multi-step DAG workflows.
bullets: Functional — One-Time & Recurring Cron Jobs: Schedule one-off delayed executions (`run_at = now + 2h`) or recurring cron schedules (`0 */6 * * *`) with timezone awareness.

Functional — Configurable Retries & Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ): Support exponential backoff with jitter (`initial=1s, factor=2.0, max_attempts=5`) and route permanently failed executions to a tenant DLQ.

Functional — Job Cancellation, Pause & Status Inspection: Allow tenants to cancel or pause a job prior to execution and query historical execution logs (`QUEUED`, `RUNNING`, `SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED`, `TIMED_OUT`).
Functional — Lease Heartbeats & DAG Chaining: Support long-running jobs via periodic worker heartbeats and trigger child jobs upon parent completion.
Non-Functional — High Timing Precision: P99 dispatch lag (difference between scheduled `next_run_at` and actual push to worker queue) < 500 milliseconds.

Non-Functional — At-Least-Once Execution with Safe Idempotency: 99.99% availability; zero dropped executions (`at-least-once` delivery) paired with fencing tokens and idempotency keys to achieve `effectively-once` side effects.
Out of Scope: Building the container hypervisor/Kubernetes kubelet itself (workers execute HTTP webhooks, gRPC calls, or pre-registered serverless task handlers).

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the platform for a multi-tenant cloud infrastructure provider scheduling billing cycles, reminder notifications, ETL pipelines, and cache warmers.
bullets: Total Registered Active Jobs: 500 Million active recurring/delayed job definitions across 100,000 tenant accounts.
Daily Job Executions: 10 Billion job executions triggered per day.

Read:Write Ratio: Each job execution produces ~4 state writes (`SCHEDULED` -> `DISPATCHED` -> `RUNNING` -> `SUCCEEDED` + next cron slot insertion) and ~2 status/poll reads (~1:2 read-to-write ratio, heavily write-intensive).
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 5x spike at top-of-the-hour (`00:00`) and top-of-the-minute boundaries because humans overwhelmingly write cron expressions like `0 * * * *` or `0 0 * * *`.
Payload Sizes: Job definition metadata = 1 KB; Schedule bucket index entry = 128 bytes; Execution history record = 512 bytes.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: The defining challenge of a job scheduler is the **Top-of-the-Hour Cron Spike**: millions of recurring jobs fire at `XX:00:00`, requiring smooth pre-fetching into memory wheels and partitioned queue buffers.
bullets: Execution Trigger QPS: 10 Billion executions / 86,400s = ~115,740 executions/sec average -> 578,700 executions/sec at 5x top-of-the-hour burst.
Database State Mutation Write QPS: 115,740 executions/sec * 4 state transitions = ~463,000 writes/sec average (batched via Kafka and asynchronous bulk upserts).

Timing Wheel & Lease Cache Memory (RAM): Pre-fetching 2 minutes of upcoming executions at peak (578,700/sec * 120s = ~69.4M upcoming tasks) * 256 bytes per wheel slot entry = ~17.8 GB RAM distributed across 64 Poller coordinator nodes (~280 MB per node).

5-Year Storage (Job Metadata + Execution Audit History): 500M active jobs * 1 KB = 500 GB. Execution logs = 10B/day * 512 B = 5.12 TB/day. Retention policy: keep hot in CockroachDB/Cassandra for 14 days (71.7 TB), and archive compressed (5:1 Zstd) to S3 for 5 years (1.02 TB/day * 1,825 days = 1.86 PB).
Network Bandwidth: Dispatch Ingress/Egress = 578,700 peak tasks/sec * 1 KB payload = ~578 MB/sec peak across the Kafka and Worker fleet.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture decouples **Schedule Discovery** (Poller nodes scanning time-bucketed shards and loading a `HashedWheelTimer`) from **Task Execution** (stateless Worker pools consuming prioritized Kafka topics and maintaining leases).
bullets: Shard Coordinator (Etcd / ZooKeeper): Assigns the 256 logical `shardId`s across the 64 active Poller nodes using ephemeral leases. If Poller Node 7 crashes, its 4 shards are immediately reassigned to surviving Poller nodes within 3 seconds.

Two-Tier Time Resolution (Minute Bucket DB + In-Memory HashedWheelTimer): The database only groups jobs by `minute_bucket` (`epoch_ms / 60000`). A Poller queries all tasks in `(current_minute, shard_id)` once every few seconds and loads them into a Netty `HashedWheelTimer` (512 ticks, 100ms resolution) to fire each task at its exact millisecond timestamp.
Priority Kafka Queues: Prevents noisy-neighbor batch jobs from delaying latency-sensitive user reminders by splitting topics into `tasks-p0-realtime`, `tasks-p1-standard`, and `tasks-p2-batch`.

Lease Reaper & Retry Engine: Background scanner that detects `RUNNING` executions whose `leaseExpiresAt < NOW()`, increments `fencingToken`, and schedules an exponential backoff retry or moves the job to the Dead-Letter Queue.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let us trace: (1) Partitioned Minute-Bucket Polling into an In-Memory Hierarchical Timing Wheel, and (2) Worker Lease Acquisition, Heartbeat Extension, Zombie Fencing, and Next Cron Slot Calculation.
bullets: Flow 1 (Time-Bucket Polling + Timing Wheel Dispatch): Instead of running `SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= NOW()` across 500M rows, a Poller node responsible for `shardId = 42` queries `WHERE minute_bucket = 29841200 AND shard_id = 42 AND claimed = false LIMIT 5000`. It marks them claimed, inserts `JobExecution` rows with `fencingToken = attemptNo`, and schedules each task inside an in-memory `HashedWheelTimer` for `delay = nextRunAtMs - System.currentTimeMillis()`. When the wheel tick fires, the task is published to Kafka.

Flow 2 (Worker Lease, Zombie Fencing & Cron Roll-Forward): When Worker A pulls the task from Kafka, it sets `status = RUNNING` and `leaseExpiresAt = NOW() + 30s`, renewing it every 10s. If Worker A suffers a 45-second JVM stop-the-world GC pause, its lease expires. The Lease Reaper marks attempt 1 `TIMED_OUT` and spawns attempt 2 with `fencingToken = 2` on Worker B. When Worker A wakes up from GC and tries to call the downstream service or mark its execution complete, the downstream service and scheduler DB reject `fencingToken = 1 < 2`.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To survive top-of-the-hour cron thundering herds and noisy multi-tenant workloads, production schedulers layer in jitter, quotas, and DAG state machines.
bullets: Deterministic Cron Smearing (Fuzzy Cron): When tenants register `@hourly` or `0 0 * * *` jobs that do not require exact-second wall-clock precision, hash the `jobId` to add a deterministic offset `hash(jobId) % 60` seconds, smoothing the midnight spike by 60x.

Per-Tenant Token Bucket Quotas & Fair Queuing: Enforce per-tenant concurrency limits in Redis so a single tenant scheduling 5 million backfill webhooks at 12:00 PM cannot starve other tenants' P0 payment jobs.

Downstream Circuit Breaking (Adaptive Backpressure): If a tenant's target webhook endpoint starts returning HTTP 503/429s, automatically trip a per-endpoint circuit breaker and pause dispatching slots for that endpoint rather than saturating worker threads on connection timeouts.

Old Minute-Bucket Partition Drop (`DROP PARTITION`): Because `schedule_slots` is range-partitioned by `minute_bucket`, completed minute partitions older than 2 hours can be dropped via an $O(1)$ metadata operation rather than expensive row-by-row `DELETE` vacuuming.

Multi-Region Active-Passive / Active-Active Failover: Replicate `JobDefinition` and `ScheduleSlot` across regions via CockroachDB/Spanner so if `us-east-1` loses power, `us-west-2` Pollers immediately claim the orphaned shards.

tradeOffs.option: Time-Bucketed Sharded DB (`minute_bucket, shard_id`) + In-Memory Timing Wheel
tradeOffs.pros: Durable across node crashes, scales linearly by adding shard IDs, avoids massive DB index scans, and delivers sub-100ms precision via `HashedWheelTimer`.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires two-stage handoff (DB poll every few seconds into in-memory wheel, then push to Kafka).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Cloud-scale distributed schedulers with 100M+ jobs and strict durability guarantees.

tradeOffs.option: Redis Sorted Sets (`ZADD schedule <timestamp> <jobId>`)
tradeOffs.pros: Ultra-fast sub-millisecond `ZRANGEBYSCORE` polling and simple implementation.
tradeOffs.cons: RAM-bound for 500M+ large job payloads, and Redis asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged jobs during a primary node crash.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Medium-scale delayed message queues (< 20M active tasks) where occasional failover loss is acceptable.

tradeOffs.option: Single Relational Table with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
tradeOffs.pros: Zero external coordination (no Etcd/ZooKeeper or Timing Wheel needed); ACID simplicity.
tradeOffs.cons: B-Tree index bloat and MVCC vacuuming bottleneck severely above ~10,000 executions/sec.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Monolithic or departmental job queues (< 5,000 QPS).

subtopics.title: Metrics / Logging System
subtopics.subtitle: Designing a planet-scale observability platform (Datadog / Prometheus + Loki) with Gorilla XOR TSDB compression, inverted label indexes, and streaming alert evaluation
keyTakeaways: Prevent High-Cardinality Tag Explosion from crashing TSDB memory: decouple unique label combinations into a 64-bit `series_id` mapped via an Inverted Index (Roaring Bitmaps), and enforce per-tenant active time-series cardinality quotas at the ingestion edge.

Achieve 12x compression on time-series samples (16 bytes -> ~1.37 bytes/sample) using Facebook Gorilla encoding (Delta-of-Delta timestamps + XOR floating-point values) inside 2-hour immutable in-memory/disk blocks.

Store logs cost-effectively (Grafana Loki / ClickHouse pattern) by indexing only low-cardinality metadata labels (`service`, `env`, `region`, `level`) while streaming compressed log chunks (Zstd columnar blocks) directly to Object Storage (S3) with Bloom filters for fast full-text needle searches.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: Modern cloud-native infrastructure requires a unified observability platform capable of ingesting tens of millions of metric data points and terabytes of structured application logs per second while powering real-time dashboards and sub-minute anomaly alerts.
bullets: Functional — Metrics Ingestion & Multi-Dimensional Tagging: Ingest counters, gauges, and histograms tagged with key-value labels (e.g., `http_requests_total{service="checkout", region="us-east", status="500"}`).

Functional — Structured Log Ingestion & Search: Ingest structured JSON logs and support filtering by label selectors (`{service="checkout", level="ERROR"}`) combined with full-text substring/regex search (`|= "NullPointerException"`).

Functional — PromQL / Time-Series Querying & Downsampling: Support range queries, aggregations (`sum by (region) (rate(...[5m]))`), and automatic historical rollups (raw 10s resolution for 15 days -> 1m resolution for 90 days -> 1h resolution for 2+ years).

Functional — Real-Time Alerting Engine: Continuously evaluate threshold and rate-of-change rules over sliding windows, deduplicate flapping alerts, and route notifications to PagerDuty, Slack, and webhooks.

Non-Functional — Write-Always Availability & Low Query Latency: 99.99% ingestion availability (observability must stay up when production is burning!); P99 dashboard query latency < 500ms for recent 6-hour windows; alert evaluation lag < 15 seconds.
Non-Functional — High Compression & Cost Efficiency: Eventual consistency of 2–5 seconds on ingestion visibility is acceptable in exchange for massive batching and 10x+ storage compression.
Out of Scope: Distributed request tracing span flamegraphs (Jaeger/Tempo UI) and Real User Monitoring (RUM) session replay video capture.

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the platform for a large cloud enterprise monitoring 500,000 hosts and 10 Million ephemeral Kubernetes containers.
bullets: Monitored Fleet & Active Time Series: 10 Million containers emitting 50 distinct metrics each = 500 Million active time series (`series_id` combinations) collected every 10 seconds.
Log Volume per Day: 10 Million containers emitting an average of 20 log lines/sec = 200 Million log events/sec (~500 bytes raw JSON per log line).
Read:Write Ratio: Extremely write-heavy (~1,000:1 writes to dashboard/alert reads). Over 95% of ingested telemetry is never queried directly after the first 2 hours unless an incident occurs.
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 3x surge during cascading production outages (when error logs explode and hundreds of engineers open live dashboards simultaneously).

Payload Sizes: Raw metric sample = 16 bytes (8B `int64` timestamp + 8B `float64` value) -> compressed via Gorilla to **1.37 bytes/sample**; Raw log line = 500 bytes -> compressed via Zstd columnar chunking (8:1 ratio) to **~62.5 bytes/log**.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: Without Gorilla time-series encoding and Zstd columnar log compression, storing 50 million metric samples/sec and 200 million log lines/sec for 5 years would bankrupt any organization.
bullets: Metrics Ingestion QPS: 500 Million active series / 10-second scrape interval = 50,000,000 samples/sec average -> 150,000,000 samples/sec at 3x peak (batched at 1,000 samples per gRPC OTLP request = 50,000 RPC/sec avg).
Log Ingestion QPS: 200,000,000 log lines/sec average (100 GB/sec raw uncompressed text -> 12.5 GB/sec on the wire with agent-side Zstd compression).

TSDB Head Block Memory (RAM): 500 Million active time series * (128 bytes series metadata/inverted index overhead + 2-hour Gorilla chunk buffer of 720 samples * 1.37 B = ~1,115 bytes per series) = ~557.5 GB total Head Block RAM across the TSDB Ingester fleet (e.g., 100 nodes * 16 GB RAM each, with RF=3 = 300 nodes).

5-Year Storage (Downsampled Metrics + Tiered Logs): Metrics raw (15-day retention) = 50M/s * 86,400s * 1.37 B = 5.92 TB/day (88.8 TB for 15d); 1-minute rollup (min/max/sum/count = 32B/min -> ~5.5B compressed/min) = 3.96 TB/day -> 5 years = 7.22 PB. Logs (30-day hot/warm S3 retention + 5-year compliance audit subset of 10% critical logs): 200M/s * 62.5 B = 12.5 GB/s = 1.08 PB/day compressed (32.4 PB for 30 days; 10% audit logs for 5 years = 108 TB/day * 1,825 = 197 PB S3 Glacier).
Network Bandwidth: Agent-compressed Ingress = ~68.5 MB/s (metrics) + 12.5 GB/s (logs) = ~12.57 GB/s (100.5 Gbps) across regional ingestion endpoints.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture follows the modern **Cortex / Thanos / Grafana Mimir & Loki** split: stateless Distributors validate and hash incoming batches; Ingesters buffer the latest 2 hours in a disk-backed Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and Gorilla memory chunks before flushing immutable blocks to S3; and Queriers federate real-time RAM state with historical S3 blocks.
bullets: DaemonSet Collector Agent (OTel / Vector): Runs on every host. Buffers telemetry in a local ring buffer, strips accidental PII/secrets via regex, pre-aggregates high-frequency counters over 10s windows, and compresses batches with Zstd.

Cardinality Guard & Distributor: Protects the cluster against a developer accidentally putting `user_id` or `request_id` into a metric label (which would spawn 100M+ useless series). Tracks active series per tenant using HyperLogLog / Redis sets and drops or strips offending labels when a tenant exceeds their quota.

TSDB Ingester (2-Hour Head Block + WAL): Appends samples to a local disk WAL for crash recovery and compresses them in memory using Gorilla XOR encoding. Every 2 hours, cuts an immutable block (Index + Chunks + Tombstones) and uploads it to S3.

Query Frontend & Federated Querier: Splits multi-day PromQL queries into 1-day sub-queries, checks a Redis step-aligned result cache, and fans out across Ingesters (for data `< 2h` old) and Store Gateways (for S3 blocks `> 2h` old).

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let us examine the two core algorithmic pillars of a time-series and logging engine: (1) Facebook Gorilla Delta-of-Delta & XOR Floating-Point Compression, and (2) Roaring Bitmap Inverted Index Intersection for Multi-Dimensional Tag Queries.
bullets: Flow 1 (Gorilla Time-Series Compression): Because metrics are scraped every 10 seconds (`t0=1000, t1=1010, t2=1020`), the delta between timestamps (`10s`) is almost always identical, meaning the **Delta-of-Delta** (`(t2 - t1) - (t1 - t0)`) is `0`! We store a `0` delta-of-delta as a single `0` bit. Similarly, consecutive IEEE-754 `double` values (e.g., CPU usage `42.15%` -> `42.15%` or `42.16%`) share almost all leading and trailing bits when XORed (`v_n ^ v_{n-1}`). If the XOR result is `0`, we write a single `0` bit; otherwise we encode only the meaningful middle bits, shrinking 16-byte `(timestamp, value)` pairs down to **1.37 bytes**.

Flow 2 (Inverted Index Roaring Bitmap Query Execution): When an engineer runs `sum(rate(http_errors{service="checkout", region="us-east"}[5m]))`, the Ingester/Querier does not scan 500M series. It looks up the Roaring Bitmap for `service="checkout"` and the Roaring Bitmap for `region="us-east"`, performs a hardware SIMD bitwise `AND` (`bitmap1.and(bitmap2)`) in microseconds to obtain the exact matching `seriesId` integers, and reads only their contiguous Gorilla byte chunks.
